title: UniqSketch: sensitive and resource-efficient strain-level detection in metagenomes
abstract: Microbial communities contain diverse organisms, including multiple coexisting strains of the same species that display phenotypic differences influencing pathogenicity and host interactions. Detecting strains is challenging because of computational demands and their low abundance in metagenomes. We present UniqSketch, an open-source toolkit for identifying target strains across species within a single metagenome. It tracks specific microbial signatures or contaminants even in complex, multi-species samples. UniqSketch uses unique genomic fingerprints and a compact Bloom filter for efficient computation and accurate abundance estimation. Results show improved precision and accuracy over existing tools, with reliable performance at sequencing coverage as low as 0.1×.

title: EnzyREx: deep learning enables reaction-based comprehensive enzyme screening
abstract: Orphan enzymes for which the corresponding genes remain unidentified represent a major gap in functional annotation in genomic analysis. We present EnzyREx, an AI-based framework for comprehensive enzyme screening, to explore novel enzyme candidates. EnzyREx consists of two deep learning models to classify proteins as enzymes and non-enzymes and predict catalytic capability for enzyme‒reaction pairs. Both models achieved performance comparable to or better than that of existing software. When applied to 1,255 microbiome-related orphan reactions, EnzyREx identified candidate proteins for 897 reactions. EnzyREx provides a scalable approach for linking unannotated proteins to orphan reactions and extending functional annotation.

title: AMR GeoMapper: client-side geospatial and temporal visualization of user-provided antimicrobial resistance data
abstract:
Background
                      Geographic visualization is a key method for monitoring the profile of global antimicrobial resistance (AMR). While current mapping tools are capable, they lack the ability to visualize or compare to user-provided data. To address this gap, we have developed and deployed AMR GeoMapper (AMR-GM) to  https://camra.acegid.org/amr-geomapper/ . AMR-GM is a web-based tool that allows for client-side geographic and temporal analysis of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) metadata. 
                  
                     Results
                      AMR-GM is a tool that enables users to produce interactive charts and maps of AMR genotypic/phenotypic and bacterial abundance data. Data can be easily formatted for AMR-GM by following the standards specified in the documentation. Additionally, AMR-GM natively loads data downloaded from amr.watch, allowing users to compare their data with publicly available datasets. The source code and documentation for AMR-GM is freely available at  https://github.com/JCVenterInstitute/AMR-GeoMapper-Public . 
                  
                     Conclusions
                      AMR-GM allows for private analysis of AMR data without reliance on public databases, giving researchers quicker access to high-quality visualizations. Because analysis of unpublished data is possible with AMR-GM, public health officials and researchers will have better software tools for analysis and surveillance of AMR and AMR pathogen spread in a geospatial framework.

title: Comparative genomics of canonical antifungal dsRNA target genes across fungal plant pathogens: conserved siRNA-length windows define the scope for broad-spectrum spray-induced gene silencing
authors: Wasif, M., Khan, M. A., Azmat, M. A., Tarcali, G., Saleem, H.
abstract: Background. Spray-induced gene silencing (SIGS), in which double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) sprayed onto a crop is taken up by a fungal pathogen and silences an essential gene, is advancing as a biopesticide strategy. A recurring ambition is a broad-spectrum dsRNA: a single construct, directed at a conserved housekeeping gene, that controls several pathogens at once. Because silencing is driven by Dicer-processed small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) of roughly 21 nucleotides, the feasibility of this ambition depends on whether the target gene is conserved between pathogens at siRNA-length resolution, not merely at the level of overall gene identity. That resolution has not been mapped across the fungal plant-pathogen tree. Results. We screened eleven canonical antifungal dsRNA target genes of Fusarium graminearum (three CYP51 sterol 14-alpha-demethylases, six chitin synthases and two beta-tubulins) for perfect 21-nucleotide identity against the transcriptomes of twelve fungal plant pathogens spanning four taxonomic classes (Sordariomycetes, Leotiomycetes, Dothideomycetes and Basidiomycota). Of 27,116 candidate siRNA start positions across the eleven genes, only 2,108 (7.8%) were conserved as a perfect 21-mer in even one other pathogen, 148 in at least three, twelve in at least seven, and none in eight or more. Conservation decayed steeply with phylogenetic distance: the congeneric F. oxysporum shared 1,209 sites, other Sordariomycetes 262-313, Leotiomycetes and Dothideomycetes 62-204, Basidiomycota 41-48, and the reduced-genome obligate biotroph Blumeria graminis just one. The beta-tubulins carried the most broadly conserved individual sites (shared by up to seven pathogens), whereas CYP51C was the least conserved (shared by at most one). Even for the congener, perfect-match conservation covered only 4.5% of target positions and was concentrated in discrete windows rather than spread along the gene. Conclusions. At the siRNA-length resolution that governs silencing, perfect-match conservation of canonical antifungal targets is scarce and strongly clade-limited. A perfect-match broad-spectrum dsRNA is therefore realistic only within a narrow clade, in practice around the genus level; genus- and class-spanning broad-spectrum SIGS cannot rely on perfect siRNA identity and would require mismatch-tolerant design or pathogen-specific constructs. The conserved windows mapped here identify where clade-level broad-spectrum constructs can be placed, and the gene ranking (beta-tubulins most cross-targetable, CYP51C most pathogen-specific) provides a genome-guided basis for choosing antifungal dsRNA targets.

title: Consensus methods for trees of blobs and level-1 phylogenetic networks
authors: Wicke, K., Banos, H., Holtgrefe, N., Allman, E. S., Ane, C., Gascuel, O.
abstract: Phylogenetic networks are increasingly used to represent evolutionary histories involving hybridization, introgression, and other reticulate processes that cannot be captured by a single tree. Recent advances have produced numerous methods for inferring networks from genomic data. These methods may produce multiple plausible networks due to optimality ties, bootstrap analyses, Bayesian posterior samples, or differences in tools, datasets, and parameters. While consensus methods are well established for trees and some approaches exist for rooted networks, no consensus framework currently exists for semi-directed (unrooted) networks. We address this gap by introducing a new consensus framework for phylogenetic networks, rooted or semi-directed. We first develop a method for constructing a consensus tree of blobs, taking as input networks of any complexity. Building on this approach, we construct a consensus for level-1 networks (i.e., networks with non-overlapping cycles). This method, called 'L1N consensus', takes a collection of level-1 networks as input and returns a level-1 network. The different components of this consensus network (e.g., blobs, hybrid clades, and edges) have support values that correspond to the frequency of the given component among the input networks. These methods are implemented in PhyloSummaries, building on the foundation of PhyloNetworks. We evaluate the performance of L1N consensus using large-scale simulated data. Our results demonstrate that L1N consensus outperforms existing methods in the rooted setting in terms of informativity and accuracy. Similar results are obtained in the semi-directed setting. Applying L1N consensus to Leopardus and HIV datasets confirms these findings and demonstrates the usefulness of the method.

title: Top2All: Benchmarking sparse-to-transcriptome reconstruction from high-expression profiles across sex- and sex-steroid-defined conditions
authors: Nishio, Y., Yamashita, T., Baba, T.
abstract: Transcriptome-wide profiling at single-cell resolution is limited by sparse detection of gene expression, raising the question of how much transcriptomic information can be recovered from a small set of highly expressed genes. We developed Top2All, a Mouse-Geneformer-based framework for reconstructing transcriptome-wide expression from sample-specific sparse inputs. Using 24 cell-number-normalized RNA-seq profiles of mouse adrenal zona fasciculata cells across eight experimental conditions defined by sex and sex-steroid milieu, we evaluated condition-aware and no-condition models under replicate-wise out-of-fold and leave-one-condition-out validation. Top2All achieved near-unity sample-wise correlation with measured expression, but similarly high correlations were obtained using simple reference profiles, whereas gene-wise evaluation revealed substantially greater differences among methods. Explicit condition information did not consistently improve reconstruction, indicating that sex- and sex-steroid-associated condition information was already strongly encoded in the sparse expression profiles. Nearest-neighbor retrieval provided a stronger baseline than learned reconstruction, and input-depth analysis showed that increasing the number of input genes did not monotonically improve performance. These findings show that a relatively small set of highly expressed genes contains substantial information about transcriptomic state, while accurate reconstruction of gene-specific biological variation remains challenging. Sparse-to-transcriptome models should therefore be evaluated using gene-wise metrics, strong reference baselines, and tests of generalization beyond conditions represented during training.

title: SENgEAR: an interactive visualization platform for comparative analysis of senescence signatures and cellular communication
authors: Nagaraj, S., Adkins, R. S., Rindone, A. N., Das, A., Lesperance, D., Orvis, J., Krishnan, K., Cosgrove, B. D., Basisty, N., Baker, D. J., White, O. R., Mahurkar, A. A., Elisseeff, J. H., Fertig, E. J.
abstract: Single-cell and spatial transcriptomic datasets provide tremendous potential to identify the cellular states and communication networks associated with senescence. Annotating senescent cells in these datasets is hindered by the lack of universal markers for senescent cells and their context-dependent variability. To overcome this, several groups have developed gene signatures to annotate cells with distinct senotypes. However, comparing these signatures and their biological contexts to determine the specificity of senescence signatures remains complicated by the separate data platforms for signatures and datasets. We present SENgEAR, a no-code web platform for senescent cell annotation, visualization of cell-cell communication networks, and comparison of senescence signatures across studies, tissues, species, and data modalities. SENgEAR provides a unified framework to explore contextual signature specificity, cellular communication pathways, and senotype heterogeneity. We demonstrate the use of SENgEAR for applications spanning aging, fibrosis, and wound healing and its ability to interrelate these states.

title: NEPTUNE: a neuronal cell death pathway prediction tool used to decipher neurodegeneration using single cell RNA-seq datasets
authors: Padvi, A. P., Brunet, A. A., Miller, A. L., Carvalho, L. S.
abstract: In the constantly evolving landscape of cell death mechanisms, much of the literature is dominated by research performed in cancer cells and regenerating cell types. However, neurons differ in that they are non-regenerating and post-mitotic. Therefore, assessing neuronal specific disease biomarkers, including cell death markers, without the bias of non-neuronal or cancerous cells, could provide a more biologically accurate neurodegeneration profile. In this study, we developed the Neuronal cEll death Prediction Tool for Understanding Neurodegenerative Events (NEPTUNE), a user-friendly tool for researchers that bioinformatically identifies neuronal cell death markers from user provided differentially expressed gene lists obtained by single cell RNA sequencing data. We applied NEPTUNE to a publicly available single cell RNA sequencing dataset and analysed the progression of photoreceptor degeneration in the rd1 mouse model of severe retinitis pigmentosa. The analysis interpreted the dataset in a neuronal-specific manner and showed that late-stage photoreceptor death is not purely apoptotic but possibly engages overlapping cell death programmes. From the analysis, the user is provided with publishable graphs and a list of cell death markers with fold change, type of impact, cell death type and a strength score. Overall, our tool provides markers specific to neurodegeneration, allows mapping to known WikiPathways and KEGG pathways, performs GO and KEGG enrichment analysis and plots the data for further analysis, greatly facilitating the study of neuron specific degeneration. The tool can be found at: https://neptune.rgtcarvalholab.com/.

title: Prefrontal cortex transcriptomes distinguish Alzheimers disease from asymptomatic amyloid pathology, neuropeptide loss, immune-complement activation and glial remodelling
authors: Munir, Y. A., Sagir, U., Sajjad, F., Khurshid, S., Tarique, F., Sani, I. M.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is now defined biologically by cortical amyloid-{beta} (A) and tau (T) pathology, yet the transcriptional programmes that separate symptomatic AD (A+T+) from amyloid-positive, tau-negative pathology ageing (A+T-) and from pathology-free controls (A-T-) remain incompletely resolved in the association cortex. We re-analysed bulk RNA-sequencing data from the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) of 15 donors (BioProject PRJNA1017546; 87 sequencing runs aggregated to donor level): Normal (n = 2), pathology ageing (n = 5) and AD (n = 8). Differential expression was tested with DESeq2 (adjusted P   1), and up- and down-regulated gene sets were analysed separately by Gene Ontology (GO) and KEGG over-representation. APOE and TREM2 p.Arg47His contrasts were treated as exploratory. AD versus Normal yielded 341 differentially expressed genes (DEGs; 223 up, 118 down) and AD versus pathology ageing yielded 496 (358 up, 138 down), whereas pathology ageing versus Normal yielded only six. Genes reduced in AD were dominated by neuropeptide and hormone signalling (VGF, VIP, CRH, GRP, TAC1, PENK; neuroactive ligand-receptor interaction, adjusted P = 8.8 x 10-5; neuropeptide hormone activity, adjusted P = 6.3 x 10-8), most of which also differed from pathology ageing. Genes increased in AD were enriched for interferon-{gamma} response, myeloid activation, adaptive immunity and classical complement (C1QA, C1QB, C1QC). Relative to pathology ageing, AD additionally showed induction of gliogenesis, oligodendrocyte differentiation and myelination programmes (gliogenesis, 21 genes, adjusted P = 2.6 x 10-6; SOX10, MYRF) and of the microglial purinergic receptor gene P2RX7 (log2FC = 1.46, adjusted P = 1.5 x 10-5). All six pathology-ageing DEGs, including the myeloid genes VSIG4 and CD163, were also DEGs in AD, and 50 DEGs shared by the two AD contrasts moved in the same direction. Genotype-stratified analyses were underpowered or confounded with diagnosis. In the DLPFC, AD is therefore characterised by a graded loss of neuropeptidergic signalling, myeloid-complement activation that begins at the pathology-ageing stage, and an AD-specific glial/oligodendrocyte response. These signatures nominate candidate biomarkers and mechanisms for early intervention, but the small cohort demands replication in larger, covariate-annotated datasets.

title: SpaceBlocks: an expert-supervised workflow for cohort-level spatial transcriptomics analysis
authors: Oterino-Sogo, S., Mechkouri, N., Garcia-Ruano, D., Groppi, A., Rezvani, H.-R., Nikolski, M.
abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) has become a central tool in tissue biology, with multiple technologies addressing the issue from a different angle. Each platform imposes its own raw data format conventions, and few workflows address reproducible, scalable, cohort-level analyses while integrating expert-supervised decisions to strengthen computational and biological provenance. In this work, we present SpaceBlocks, a Snakemake workflow for reproducible cohort-level analysis of single-cell resolution-ST data that prioritizes expert supervision over full automation. SpaceBlocks homogenizes heterogeneous platform outputs into a common data format, whose structure is validated to ensure downstream processing. Comprehensive expert supervision is facilitated through per sample quality control and cell type annotation diagnostic visualizations, after which downstream analyses automatically follow. SpaceBlocks also allows the ingestion of technology-agnostic externally formatted data and provides interoperability with existing tools and technologies. We demonstrate the use of SpaceBlocks through the reanalysis of 37 samples from public Visium HD, Xenium 5K and MERSCOPE datasets. SpaceBlocks exhibited processing scalability across the three platforms. This reanalysis identified previously missed cell types in Visium HD and heterogeneous marker gene expression in MERSCOPE, highlighting the need for expert-supervised annotations. Moreover, SpaceBlocks facilitated the identification of differentially expressed genes associated with previously defined multiple sclerosis (MS) spatial domains in MERSCOPE, and transcriptional differences between healthy and malignant colorectal tissues in Visium HD. Together, these findings establish SpaceBlocks as a flexible and reproducible workflow for expert-supervised spatial transcriptomics analysis across technologies and biological cohorts.

title: Quantifying heritability in functional regions of the coding and non-coding genome across diverse individuals
authors: Lupu, T. V., Wright, H. I. W., Armirola-Ricaurte, C., Huerta-Chagoya, A., Wood, A. R., Mercader, J. M., Manning, A. K., Hysong, M., Barroso, I., Wright, C. F., Weedon, M. N., Beaumont, R. N., Chundru, V. K., Hawkes, G.
abstract: Most heritability studies have focused on common genetic variation and have largely excluded non-European or highly admixed populations. Here, we estimated the whole-genome heritability (h2WGS) of seven complex traits using 73,600,953 autosomal and chromosome X variants for 198,931 unrelated individuals from three genetic similarity groups. Adjusting for population stratification, we showed that rare variants (minor allele frequency<0.01) explain 30.6-67.7% of h2WGS. We used simulations to show how functionally-stratified heritability can be inflated due to linkage with missing or lower-quality variants. Finally, after accounting for confounding effects, we found substantial heritability enrichment from variants in non-coding RNA exons (maximum fold enrichment, FE=8.7, P=3.56e-7), UTRs (23.0, P=3.46e-30), distal regulatory regions (33.8, P=3.26e-42), and protein-coding exons (58.0, P=7.78e-15). Our study provides a framework for investigating the genetic architecture of complex human phenotypes using diverse whole-genome sequencing data and highlights the contribution of rare and non-coding genetic variants to the heritability of complex traits.

title: CMVAE: Contrastive Supervision Improves Single-Omic Latent Manifold for Breast Cancer Survival Prognosis
authors: Singh, A., Kohut, A., Templeton, J. M., Kabir, A.
abstract: High-dimensional omics data are vital for fore- casting patient prognosis in oncology. While deep multi-omics learning methods are increasingly popular, they suffer from data missingness and low patient overlap across modalities. Consequently, advancing single-omic representation learning re- mains a critical yet challenging research problem. Standard generative dimensionality reduction methods rely on recon- struction objectives that optimize the global manifold topology; however, overlook downstream clinical outcomes. To address these limitations, we introduce a Contrastive Masked Denois- ing Variational Autoencoder (CMVAE), a self-supervised dual- optimization framework designed to map single-omic information into a clinical outcome-aware latent space. A stochastic feature masking strategy corrupts the input omic profiles, and CMVAE is optimized to simultaneously infer missing molecular data and contrastive alignment of patient survival trajectories. We evaluate CMVAE using leak-proof five-fold stratified cross-validation on the TCGA Breast Invasive Carcinoma (BRCA) cohort. The method outperforms traditional unsupervised methods, achieving an AUROC of 0.7397 {+/-} 0.0239 on patient prognosis. Further analysis demonstrates a highly significant (p < 0.0001) risk stratification among low vs. high risk groups. Beyond comparing within single-omic methods, CMVAE outperforms six state-of- the-art multi-omics survival baselines by a minimum of 3%. Availability: All codes including data preparation scripts, training and validation recipes, and experimental configurations are available at: https://github.com/kabir-ai2bio-lab/CMVAE. Note: Accepted at the IEEE BIBM 2026 workshop RLPD-Bio (Representation Learning and Pattern Discovery for Bioinformatics and Biomedicine).

title: MaCADEMIA: a software toolbox for single-molecule fluorescence image quantification
authors: Alderson, D., Catchpole, Z., Crompton, K., Sanders, K., Johnson, S., Smith, K., Packer, J., Harris, K. S., Rodriguez, J., Leake, M. C., Wollman, A. J.
abstract: Single-molecule localisation microscopy (SMLM) is a powerful tool in molecular and cellular biology and part of the broad umbrella of super-resolution microscopy. A distinct feature of SMLM, is its capacity for deep quantification, beyond just spatial information, to copy number, stoichiometry, molecular interaction and dynamics in living cells. The hardware required is increasingly straightforward to implement. However, complexity remains in the image analysis where much remains fragmented across specialised software tools. Here, we present MaCADEMIA (Matlab Computational Analysis of Diffusion, Emitter Molecular Intensity and Abundance), a simple yet powerful toolbox of MATLAB functions and associated documentation to enable straightforward extraction of quantitative single-molecule information. MaCADEMIA performs ensemble particle detection achieving localisation accuracies down to 0.5 pixels Root mean squared error (RMSE) across wide signal-to-noise (SNR) ranges on standardised particle tracking benchmarks, consistently matching or exceeding the performance of 14 leading methods. Our integrated workflow enables molecular counting and stoichiometry determination through stepwise photobleaching analysis, mobility measurement via mean squared displacement, colocalisaton analysis and absolute protein copy number quantification using three-dimensional cellular models.

title: Leakage-Controlled Benchmarking of Variant Effect Predictors and Development of Gradient-Boosting Consensus Model
authors: Havlasek, M., Kabourek, P., Musil, M., Damborsky, J., Mazurenko, S., Bednar, D.
abstract: Single amino acid mutations are among the most common forms of genetic variation, with effects ranging from negligible to severe disruption of protein function. Accurate quantitative evaluation of protein variants therefore represents a key challenge in medicine and protein engineering. Computational variant effect predictors (VEPs) are widely used to prioritize missense variants, yet their fair comparison is hindered by data circularity, benchmarks restricted to human clinical annotations, and limited availability of code and training data, all of which can inflate apparent performance. Here, we reviewed 18 recent and 3 older, widely adopted variant effect predictors for reproducible benchmarking and assembled a rigorously curated, leakage-controlled Benchmark dataset by integrating clinically annotated human variants from ClinVar and Humsavar as well as cross-species variants with functional annotations. The evaluation on this dataset revealed a narrow overall performance range for the benchmarked tools (AUC 0.631-0.758) and a consistent drop from clinical to functional data. Surprisingly, several tools published two decades ago demonstrated comparable performance to mid-ranked modern predictors. Building on these results, we developed a gradient-boosting consensus model, PredictSNPprot, which achieved an AUC of 0.82 on a held-out test set, outperforming the original PredictSNP meta-predictor and the best individual state-of-the-art tool by 13.6 and 5.7 percentage points, respectively. The Benchmark dataset, including the predictions from the evaluated tools, is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23597130 and PredictSNPprot consensus predictor is available at https://github.com/loschmidt/PredictSNPprot.

title: The Almond Expression Atlas: A comprehensive multi-tissue transcriptomic resource for almond gene expression
authors: Lopez-Fernandez, E. M., Zwieniecki, M., Tixier, A., Botia, J. A., Martinez-Garcia, P. J.
abstract: Background: Improving crop adaptation and enhancing agronomic and quality traits requires a deeper understanding of gene expression regulation, for which expression atlases are valuable tools. Almond (Prunus dulcis (Mill.) D.A. Webb) is one of the most economically important tree nut crops worldwide. However, an integrated transcriptomic resource for this species is still lacking. Available data remain fragmented across independent studies, limiting their comparability and reuse. Results: Here, we present the first almond gene expression atlas: a comprehensive multi-tissue transcriptomic resource integrating publicly available RNA sequencing data. A total of 142 high-quality untreated and control samples from 17 independent projects were curated through a metadata standardization process and analyzed using a unified bioinformatics pipeline. Standardized expression profiles were generated for 25,225 annotated genes in the Prunus dulcis Texas v2.0 reference genome. The atlas integrates two complementary expression approaches: a median TPM approach capturing quantitative expression levels and a rank-based strategy implemented using the Bgee expression calling method, designed to improve comparability across heterogeneous datasets. This design enables the identification of tissue-specific candidate genes and the exploration of expression patterns across tissues and developmental stages. Its applicability is demonstrated through two use cases, highlighting its ability to identify biologically meaningful gene sets associated with bud dormancy transitions and to prioritize candidate reference genes for RT-qPCR normalization in almond. Conclusions: The Almond Expression Atlas v1.0 is publicly available through FruitDBase (fruitdbase.csic.es), providing an interactive platform for gene expression exploration and visualization. This resource supports functional genomics studies and facilitates candidate gene discovery in almond, while ensuring data traceability and promoting data reusability.

title: A multidimensional benchmark of confounder-aware differential abundance strategies for single- and multi-cohort microbiome studies
authors: Zhu, X., Liu, L., Cao, Y., Sheng, Y., Yang, B., Wu, D., Zhang, G., Zhao, G., Jiao, N., Zhu, R.
abstract: Confounding is a pervasive challenge in microbiome differential abundance analysis (DAA), yet systematic benchmarks of confounder-aware DAA remain lacking. Existing benchmarks have also largely evaluated statistical methods or analytical components in isolation rather than the complete analytical strategies used in practice. We evaluated 71 single-cohort strategies spanning default and extended input configurations using 2,500 real-data-informed simulations, reference-based recovery of established biological signals and resampling-based within-dataset consistency; benchmark-prioritized strategies were further assessed for stability under systematic perturbations. We further evaluated 63 multi-cohort extensions using simulations with cohort heterogeneity and empirical datasets. Covariate adjustment improved false-discovery control at the cost of reduced sensitivity, while performance also depended strongly on the specific combination of preprocessing procedure and statistical model. Different strategies were favored across benchmark dimensions and analytical objectives. ANCOM-BC2_CSS and edgeR_CSS were favored for high-confidence, perturbation-stable inference, whereas ANCOM-BC2_count and ANCOM-BC2_TMM provided more balanced performance. In multi-cohort settings, mega-analysis provided the strongest overall balance when individual-level data were available: ANCOM-BC2_CSS_Mega and edgeR_CSS_Mega showed stronger accuracy performance, whereas ANCOM-BC2_TMM_Mega and ANCOM-BC2_count_Mega showed greater cross-cohort consistency. We implemented these findings in xConDA, an interactive web server linking analytical objectives and study designs to benchmark-prioritized, confounder-adjusted microbiome DAA workflows.

title: Ultrasensitive detection of neuronal DNA using genome-wide non-CG methylation patterns
authors: Loyfer, N., Horn, A., Hart, S., Rosenski, J., Piyanzin, S., Magenheim, J., Sabag, O., Avniel Aran, A., Langer, Y., Barsoum, N., Rosenthal, G., Gat, M., Olthoff, K., Shaked, A., Shemer, R., Glaser, B., Kaplan, T., Dor, Y.
abstract: Methylation-based liquid biopsies can identify the tissue origins of circulating cell-free DNA (cfDNA). A major constraint on the sensitivity of these assays is the limited number of cell-type-specific CpG markers. Here we exploit the high abundance of non-CpG (CpH) methylation in neurons to enable ultrasensitive detection of neuronal DNA. We show that neurons carry 100-fold higher CpH methylation than other tissues, in which apparent CpH methylation largely reflects experimental artifacts. Using a computational criterion to identify cfDNA molecules carrying clusters of methylated CpA sites, we detect neuronal DNA at proportions as low as 20 parts per million. Analysis of 231 samples from 163 individuals revealed minimal neuronal cfDNA in the plasma of healthy subjects; elevated levels in patients with measles or acute neurological conditions; strikingly high levels in brain-dead donors, indicating extensive ongoing neuronal death; and the highest levels in the cerebrospinal fluid of patients in a neurological intensive care unit. These findings establish genome-wide, fragment-level analysis of non-CpG methylation as an ultrasensitive approach for blood-based monitoring of brain injury and disease.

title: An Isogenic iPSC Model of LMNA p.R482W Recapitulates Adipocyte Dysfunction in Familial Partial Lipodystrophy Type 2
authors: Borrego Alvarez, A., Wasielewski, W. O., Gobble, M. R. S., Grupe, M., Ali, L. M., Buchser, W., Boggs-Bailey, L., Baldridge, D., Maung, J. N., Nishii, A., MacDougald, O. A., Oral, E. A., Stone, S. I.
abstract: Familial partial lipodystrophy type 2 (FPLD2) is a rare autosomal dominant disorder caused by pathogenic variants in LMNA, most commonly p.R482W, and is characterized by selective loss of subcutaneous adipose tissue, severe insulin resistance, and dyslipidemia. The cellular mechanisms underlying adipocyte dysfunction in FPLD2 remain incompletely understood, in part because existing in vitro models rely on patient-derived, non-isogenic cell lines or require non- physiologic transgene overexpression to achieve adipogenic differentiation. Here, we describe a CRISPR/Cas9-edited isogenic iPSC model of FPLD2 in which the heterozygous LMNA c.1444C>T (p.R482W) variant was introduced into a healthy donor-derived iPSC line. Using a transgene-free mesenchymal progenitor differentiation protocol, we generated LMNAp.R482W and isogenic control adipocytes and characterized their transcriptomic and functional phenotypes. Bulk RNA- sequencing demonstrated strong concordance in adipogenesis gene expression between genotypes during differentiation (Pearson {rho} = 0.968), yet LMNAp.R482W adipocytes exhibited significant downregulation of key adipogenic, lipid-handling, and extracellular matrix genes compared to isogenic controls. Functionally, LMNAp.R482W adipocytes showed markedly impaired glucose uptake under both basal and insulin-stimulated conditions, consistent with severe insulin resistance. Seahorse extracellular flux analysis revealed a globally quiescent metabolic state with significantly reduced oxygen consumption rate (126.5 vs. 261.5 pmol/min, p < 0.0001) and extracellular acidification rate (27.6 vs. 46.7 mpH/min, p < 0.0001). To validate these findings in human tissue, gene set enrichment analysis results from the iPSC model were compared to single-nucleus RNA-sequencing data from subcutaneous white adipose tissue biopsies of individuals with FPLD2 carrying the LMNA p.R482W variant. Across 37 mutually significant pathways, 59.5% were concordant between the iPSC model and human adipose tissue, including the pathways most central to FPLD2 pathophysiology: adipogenesis, fatty acid metabolism, oxidative phosphorylation, and inflammatory response. These findings establish this isogenic iPSC system as a faithful cellular model of FPLD2 adipocyte biology and a platform for functional characterization of LMNA variants of uncertain significance.

title: Refining RNA-Seq Transcriptome Profiles with Transcript-Specific Minimal-Shared Regions
abstract: Accurate transcript quantification remains a critical challenge in RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) due to ambiguities in read assignment caused by shared regions among transcripts. Beyond shared exons among homologous isoforms, we identified the widespread presence of extensive undefined shared regions-overlapping sequences common to exons or transcripts of heterologous genes-across diverse species, including animals and plants. To overcome this issue, we developed a minimal-sharing strategy that partitions transcripts into unique sets of k-mers and systematically evaluates overlap across all transcripts. By isolating minimal-shared regions specific to each isoform, our approach reduces mapping uncertainty, thereby minimizing false positives and false negatives in transcript detection. Comprehensive evaluations using both in silico simulations and empirical sequencing data demonstrated that our method outperforms traditional probabilistic model-based quantification methods. This strategy improves isoform abundance estimates, enhances gene ontology annotations, and identifies distinct transcript isoforms critical for understanding biological processes, as exemplified in a Huntington's disease mouse model.

title: GraphExperiment: infrastructure for high-dimensional quantitative data and associated networks in R/Bioconductor
abstract: Networks are widely used to represent relationships among features (e.g. genes, proteins, and microbial taxa) and among observations (e.g. cells, samples, and species) in omics data, as well as their neighborhoods. The Bioconductor ecosystem provides users and developers with modular and interoperable software tools by relying on standard data structures that are reused across packages. However, Bioconductor lacks a standard data structure to store such networks together with the quantitative data from which they are inferred. Here, we present GraphExperiment, an R/Bioconductor package that provides an S4 class extending SingleCellExperiment with containers for feature- level (rowGraphs) and observation-level (colGraphs) networks stored as igraph objects. Networks are kept in sync with assays, row and column metadata, allowing the simultaneous manipulation of quantitative data and graphs. We demonstrate GraphExperiment in seven use cases covering bulk and single-cell transcriptomics, single-cell proteomics, microbiome, and comparative genomics data, with networks ranging from gene coexpression and protein co-abundance networks to cell-cell communication and phylogenetic networks. GraphExperiment is available on Bioconductor (https://bioconductor.org/packages/GraphExperiment).

title: A Chromosome Scale Genome Assembly for the Australian blue mussel Mytilus planulatus
authors: Kireta, D., Nerelli, D. E., Saco, A., Bortoletto, E., Howitt, S., Rosani, U., Riginos, C., Gerdol, M.
abstract: Mussels belonging to the genus Mytilus are among the world's most ecologically and economically important bivalve molluscs. Although the genus most likely originated in the Northern Hemisphere, the evolutionary history of Southern Hemisphere lineages, including the timing and number of colonisation events leading to the extant Australian populations, remains debated. Limited genomic resources have hindered the reconstruction of these evolutionary histories. In Australia, distinguishing native Mytilus planulatus from invasive Mytilus galloprovincialis is critical for biosecurity and conservation, but previous molecular approaches lacked sufficient resolution to resolve species boundaries and hybridisation patterns. Here, we present the first chromosome-scale reference genome for M. planulatus. The assembly consists of 14 chromosomes and over 51,000 annotated protein-coding genes per haplotype. Comparative analysis revealed extensive structural variation and widespread hemizygosity despite a largely conserved chromosomal organisation relative to M. galloprovincialis. Population analyses using SNPs and gene presence-absence variation in resequenced individuals confirmed previously inferred patterns of population structure and establish this reference genome as a valuable resource for future studies of genome evolution, adaptation and population genomics in Mytilus.

title: A single-cell multimodal foundation model enables cross modality analysis between transcriptome and chromatin
authors: Bao, X., Zhu, J., Song, X., Zhang, X., Zeng, H., Vu, H. T. H., Zhang, H., Zhang, Z., Yao, M., Liang, M., Liu, K., Parker, S. C., Chen, S., Liu, J.
abstract: Most single-cell studies measure either gene expression or chromatin accessibility, and connecting the two usually requires fitting a model to each study. Here we present MUTUAL (MUltiome Transfer in a Unified Aligned Latent space), which keeps the single-cell foundation models scFoundation and EpiAgent frozen, combines their embeddings with linear summaries of each modality and learns a shared RNA--ATAC space from 3.0 million paired cells of 400 public multiome datasets. Applied without refitting to ten datasets not used for training, MUTUAL matched cells' RNA and ATAC profiles more accurately than methods fitted on other donors of the same dataset, annotated ATAC-only cells more accurately and transferred transcription-factor motif activity to RNA-only cells beyond what cell-type assignment provides. In a maturation series of stem-cell-derived islets, motif activity predicted from RNA largely reproduced the measured stage-wise changes when other libraries of the series served as the reference. MUTUAL makes public multiome data directly usable by single-modality studies.

title: Multi-modal in situ profiling of human cells using the AVITI24 platform characterizes single-cell responses to acute stress
authors: Lang, O. W., Gardner, A. M., Smugereski, C. M., Lyndaker, A. M., Pugh, B. F., Lai, W.
abstract: Cells begin to respond to stress within minutes, but how this early response depends on cell type, neighboring cells, or cell cycle phase has been difficult to determine, because bulk assays average across cells and synchronization can induce stress. We measured 338 transcripts, 48 proteins and phosphoproteins, and six cell paint stains in situ in 1.18 million single cells from four human cell lines exposed to H2O2, alone and in co-culture, and in A549 cells exposed to TNF-, cadmium, dithiothreitol or lipopolysaccharide. In A549 cells, five distinct stressors changed the same targets in the same direction within 15 min, differing mainly in magnitude, and modestly increased JNK phosphorylation. By 30 min of H2O2 treatment, immediate-early genes (FOS, JUN, DDIT3, DUSP1, NR4A1) were induced most strongly in HCT116 and A549 cells. These changes occurred across the whole cell population rather than in a responsive subset. Cell line-specific differences persisted in co-culture, and the response of MCF7 cells did not increase with the number of adjacent, strongly-responding A549 cells. Ordering cells along the cell cycle from the same measurements identified 106 cycle-associated transcripts, and the response varied more between cell lines than among cell cycle phases. Overall, the measured regulators respond to stress within 30 minutes through a largely shared program whose magnitude depends more on cell identity than on cell cycle state or neighboring cell type.

title: TSNR: Protein-Specific Signals with Broad Molecular Context for Spatial Protein Prediction
abstract: Spatial transcriptomics measures transcriptome-wide gene expression while preserving tissue organization, enabling prediction of spatial protein abundance beyond directly measured antibody panels. Such prediction draws on protein-specific transcript signals at the center spot and broader molecular context from the surrounding tissue. Existing spatial methods increasingly use context, but what molecular information the context should retain and how reliably it transfers across tissue environments remain unclear.We compare predictors that share a protein-specific center representation but differ in contextual molecular scope. Their transferred risk difference admits a value-mismatch characterization: broader context is favored when its target-side value advantage exceeds the corresponding change in source-to-target transfer mismatch. For convex prediction objectives, we further relate mismatch to cross-environment estimating-score variation; squared loss yields an explicit covariance geometry. This analysis motivates broad molecular context together with bounded-score robust regression. We develop Target-Specific Niche Regression (TSNR), which combines a protein-specific center representation, compact broad molecular context, and a protein-specific Huber regressor.On the six-section Spatial-CITE-seq benchmark, TSNR achieves the highest mean macro Spearman correlation among the reproduced methods under matched biological holdout evaluation. Controlled analyses support both broader context and robust regression. Across two independent external cohorts, protein-level broad-context gains are positively rank-correlated with the value-mismatch balance in all 11 held-out biological folds.

title: Predicted condensation-related signatures localize to two C-terminal regions of the prion protein across cervid PRNP variants associated with chronic wasting disease
authors: Dayhoff, G. W., Dorosh, L., Wille, H., Uversky, V. N., Stepanova, M.
abstract: Genetic variation in cervid PRNP influences chronic wasting disease (CWD) susceptibility and progression, but it remains unclear whether disease-associated substitutions produce localized differences in sequence-derived properties relevant to prion protein (PrPC) condensation. We compared a white-tailed deer (WTD) reference sequence with 10 modeled variants on the same mature PrP scaffold (residues 24-233). For each sequence, we calculated intrinsic disorder, FuzDrop per-residue droplet-promoting propensity (pDP) and binding-mode entropy (Sbind), predicted residue-level pKa values, and a discrete-charge summary at pH 7.0. The overall profiles preserve a long N-terminal droplet-promoting region, whereas variant-associated differences are concentrated in selected intervals. In the FuzDrop outputs, residues 126-140 show allele-dependent changes in pDP near the droplet-promoting threshold, and residues 220-230 show variant-specific changes in Sbind, including lower Sbind for S225F/Y and higher Sbind for elk-like Q226E. These differences occur without large changes in overall intrinsic disorder. KaML pKa predictions identify near-neutral titratable sites that provide electrostatic context for these local predictor differences. Independent atomistic simulations of monomeric PrP further detected variant-sensitive backbone behavior and intramolecular contacts involving these intervals. Together, the analysis identifies residues 126-140 and 220-230 as computationally defined candidate intervals that overlap regions implicated independently in prion conversion or CWD fibril structure, motivating direct tests of cervid PrP condensation and maturation.

title: ToxINsight: An Integrated Web Platform for Sequence, Structure, and Ligand Binding Analysis of Snake Venom Toxins
authors: Gupta, A., Krishna, T. V. L., Singh, B.
abstract: Around 5.4 million people worldwide are bitten by snakes each year, with 1.8 to 2.7 million cases of envenomation, of which 81,410 to 137,880 people die from snake envenomation worldwide each year. It is categorized as a high-priority Category A Neglected Tropical Disease (NTD) by the World Health Organization (WHO). A molecular level understanding of snake venom toxins and their mechanisms of action is crucial for development of efficient therapeutics tackling snake envenomation. Snake venoms are complex mixtures of bioactive peptides and proteins that have also served as templates for drug discovery. Resources dedicated to snake venom toxins sequence, structure, functions, geographical distributions and molecular-level analysis remain fragmented across general-purpose repositories. Here we present ToxINsight, an integrated, freely accessible database and web-based analysis platform built exclusively for snake venom toxins. ToxINsight curates 2,078 toxin entries spanning 11 medically and scientifically relevant snake toxin families across 237 venomous snake species from five different snake families, and provides 2,540 three-dimensional structures associated with these entries, which are assembled from the RCSB Protein Data Bank , AlphaFold DB and ESMFold-generated 3D models. ToxINsight offers built-in tools alongside toxin records for comparisons and analysis of toxin sequences and structures and their properties for efficient target selection and prioritization. ToxINsight allow the user to select multiple entries and align them, or select a pair of entries to compare structural and physicochemical properties. ToxINsight provides all reported-ligand annotations for each toxin entry, and bulk export of sequence, structure, and metadata for building sequence and/or structure based machine learning models . ToxINsight also offers a visual ATLAS, which provides geographical information about venomous snake families/species for a more focused understanding of snake venom toxins across different geographical landscapes. By combining sequence, structure, ligand and geographical information along with analysis and comparative tools in a single interface, ToxINsight is designed to support and encourage researchers across the world towards the development of efficient targeted therapeutics against snake venom toxins from diverse families. It provides an interface for integrated understanding toxin sequences, structures and physicochemical properties, for providing scaffolds for designing antivenom and for comparative venomics. ToxINsight is freely accessible at https://toxinsight.in/.

title: Peripheral Exercise Transcriptomes Do Not Converge on Glutamatergic or Neuroinflammatory Signatures: A Cross-Platform Meta-Analysis
abstract: Executive dysfunction following physical overtraining has been linked to glutamatergic dysregulation in the lateral prefrontal cortex (LPFC), but whether this central mechanism is reflected in peripheral gene expression is unknown. This study tested whether peripheral transcriptomic responses to exercise converge on the glutamatergic or neuroinflammatory pathways implicated in LPFC dysfunction. Three publicly available GEO datasets spanning skeletal muscle, whole blood, and circulating neutrophils were analyzed across four exercise groups using limma, with a discovery threshold of nominal p < 0.05 and absolute log2 fold change above 0.5. Differential expression analysis identified 7,311 unique differentially expressed genes (DEGs) across the four contrasts, but overlap between datasets was limited: 7 genes were shared between skeletal muscle and blood, 38 between skeletal muscle and the GSE43856 contrasts, and 90 between blood and the GSE43856 contrasts, with none significant across all three studies. Gene Ontology and KEGG enrichment of the DEG union identified ribonucleoprotein complex biogenesis, ribosome biogenesis, protein folding, and T cell activation as the dominant biological processes; no glutamatergic or neuroinflammatory terms reached significance. Cross-tissue concordance between skeletal muscle and blood was absent (r = 0). Effect sizes among the genes driving the top enriched pathways were dominated by ribosomal proteins, heat shock proteins, and translation initiation factors rather than glutamate receptors or transporters. These findings indicate that peripheral transcriptomic responses to exercise are tissue-specific and dominated by proteostasis, translational, and immune programs rather than glutamatergic signaling. Direct assessment of central nervous system tissue or fluid-based glutamatergic biomarkers may be required to link overtraining-induced fatigue to LPFC dysfunction.

title: Local fractal dimension as an indicator of functional reorganization in molecular interaction networks
authors: Hause, F., Wedler-Geyer, A., Lederer, M., Fuchs, T., Ihling, C. H., Taenzler, D., Keil, R., Sorokin, O., Wussow, S., Sinz, A., Huettelmaier, S.
abstract: Changes in protein abundance incompletely describe how molecular perturbations reshape cellular organization. Here we introduce DIFFRACT, a framework that integrates quantitative proteomics with protein-protein interaction networks to identify reorganization through changes in local fractal dimension. Molecular associations define effective distances between connected proteins, allowing the geometry of their surrounding network neighborhoods to be compared across conditions. Analyses across four organisms (E. coli, A. thaliana, C. elegans, and H. sapiens) and three interaction resources (STRING, BioGRID, and IntAct) establish heterogeneous local scaling, while controlled perturbations demonstrate sensitivity to regional changes and invariance to uniform distance rescaling. Applied to RAVER1-deficient A549 cells, DIFFRACT identifies components associated with established RNA-regulatory functions and candidate roles in tRNA biology, mitochondrial organization and ciliogenesis. Selected RNA-regulatory and ciliary themes are not significantly enriched by abundance-ranked gene set analysis, supporting complementary information from network geometry. Selected functional annotations also recur in HEK293T cells. Guided by the ciliary predictions, we show that RAVER1 depletion increases the proportion of ciliated A549 cells 2.57-fold and increases cilium length. DIFFRACT thus connects changes in molecular network geometry to experimentally testable biological responses, extending the interpretation of proteomic perturbations beyond differential abundance.

title: Recurrent mitotic error and purifying selection shape chromosomal mosaicism across human tissues
authors: Tang, D., Kamitaki, N., Si, Y., Sexton, C. E., Feng, W. C., Veit, A. D., Chun, H.-J. E., Park, P. J., Loh, P.-R.
abstract: Mosaic chromosomal alterations (mCAs) have been extensively studied in cancer and clonal hematopoiesis but less so in healthy solid tissues. Here, we characterized mCAs in 19 tissues across 25 donors (aged 42-89+ years) by analyzing >200x whole-genome sequencing data generated by the Somatic Mosaicism across Human Tissues (SMaHT) Network. Across 722 tissue samples, we identified 1,008 autosomal mCAs >1 Mb in length and ubiquitous losses of sex chromosomes. Surprisingly, the highest levels of Y chromosome loss in males (5-10% cell fraction in elderly donors) were observed in the lung, adrenal gland, and heart. These tissues also tended to experience more X loss in females, revealing a gradient of mitotic error burden across human tissues. Autosomal aneuploidies displayed distinct tissue-specific patterns indicative of negative selection against most events, except in the adrenal gland, in which low-level aneuploidy was pervasive. In contrast to the adrenal gland, testis rarely harbored aneuploidies but frequently experienced low-level copy-neutral loss of heterozygosity (CN-LOH), suggesting increased mitotic recombination in spermatogonial stem cells. Recurrent X chromosome losses within tissues of female donors exhibited allelic skews explained by a combination of genetic and epigenetic effects. Together, these results show that the chromosomal landscape of aging human tissues is shaped by genetics and recurrent mutations, most but not all of which are held in check by purifying selection.

title: scRM: A single-cell foundation model trained on scRNA-seq reads
authors: He, D., Patro, R., Nassar, M., Wu, H., Yan, Q., Xu, G., Torkenczy, K., Liu, J., Tyanova, S.
abstract: To our knowledge, scRM is the first single-cell foundation model trained on sequencing reads, demonstrating that raw data pretraining is not only feasible but competitive at a fraction of the computational cost. We anticipate that scaling this framework and exploring alternative architectures will unlock biological information inaccessible to count models and extend the dataset-specific pretraining it already makes possible. The source code is available at https://github.com/altos-labs/scRM.

title: SpatioCAD: Context-aware graph diffusion model for pinpointing spatially variable genes in heterogeneous tissues
abstract:
by Hao Wen, Qunlun Shen, Shuqin Zhang 

Spatial transcriptomics enables comprehensive characterization of tissue architecture, and the identification of spatially variable genes (SVGs) is a critical step for defining region-specific molecular markers and uncovering spatially regulated mechanisms across diverse biological contexts. However, most existing methods for SVG detection overlook cell density variations, a major confounding factor in complex tissues such as tumors, where heterogeneous cellularity frequently introduces false-positive calls. Here we present SpatioCAD, a computational framework that explicitly decouples genuine spatial expression patterns from confounding effects driven by cellularity. SpatioCAD introduces a graph diffusion model that inherently incorporates cell-density-aware conditions to simulate expression propagation, supporting the identification of SVGs across a broad range of expression levels. Systematic evaluations on simulated datasets demonstrate its superior statistical power and specificity. Applied to breast cancer, lung cancer, and glioma datasets, SpatioCAD identifies functionally diverse SVGs, including low‑abundance transcripts with established roles in tumor progression, while also recapitulates biologically meaningful tissue architecture features. Importantly, SpatioCAD is fast and scalable to large tissues.

title: The promiscuity and degeneracy of ten unique RNA base-pairing rules can determine the success of adaptive RNA evolution
abstract:
by Leander Goldbach, Nora S. Martin, Andreas Wagner 

The topography of fitness landscapes strongly influences the outcome of Darwinian evolution. This topography in turn is determined by the effects of genotypic changes on phenotypes, such as the structure and function of biomolecules like proteins and RNA. Thus, understanding the evolution of biomolecules requires an understanding of the relationship between genotype and phenotype. Here, we study how this relationship is influenced by the fundamental biochemical rules that determine which RNA bases can form base-pairs in RNA secondary structure. To this end, we computationally study the secondary structure genotype-phenotype maps of RNA molecules using all ten possible different such RNA base-pairing rules. We simulate adaptive evolution on fitness landscapes in which an RNA’s fitness is defined by its secondary structure. We find that the base-pairing rules strongly affect how likely an evolving population is to find the global peak of a fitness landscape. The base-pairing rule of most biological RNA molecules (A-U, G-C, G-U) is among the top three most favorable rules for adaptive evolution, in which over 80% of evolving populations find a landscape’s highest fitness peak. Simple characteristics of the genotype-phenotype map, such as the fraction of genotypes that constitute local peaks can help to predict how likely evolving populations are to find a landscape’s global fitness peak. These characteristics can in turn be explained by two elementary properties of base-pairing rules that we call promiscuity and degeneracy.

title: Direction-selective retinal ganglion cells encode motion direction uniformly, despite having discretely distributed cardinal preferences
abstract:
by Carlo Paris, Félix Hubert, Felix Franke, Olivier Marre, Matthew Chalk, Ulisse Ferrari 

On-Off direction-selective retinal ganglion cells (DS RGCs) exhibit broad tuning curves, responding robustly to motion aligned with or near their preferred direction. These cells comprise four major subtypes, each tuned to motion along one of the four cardinal axes: nasal, superior, temporal, or inferior. However, natural stimuli can move in any direction, and it remains unclear whether intermediate directions are encoded less effectively, or whether this cardinal organization nevertheless supports uniform direction encoding. Here, we combined previous electrophysiological recordings of DS cells presented with a moving light bar stimulus with an information-theoretic measure, the Stimulus Specific Information, to estimate the directional sensitivity of small populations of recorded neurons. This analysis revealed that DS RGC populations are uniformly sensitive across all directions of motion. We then asked whether the observed homogeneous sensitivity was a consequence of DS RGCs maximizing the average stimulus information. Simulations with artificially modified tuning curve widths revealed that DS cells prioritize avoiding pronounced drops in sensitivity over maximizing the average transmitted information. This property reduces large deficits in sensitivity for certain directions, thereby limiting potential “blind spots” in the encoding of motion. More generally, our results raise the possibility that maintaining a high minimum sensitivity could be one factor influencing the organization of sensory representations.

title: Traction force microscopy using temporal information
abstract:
by Kazuko Hamaoka, Kasumi Kusakari, Hirokazu Tanimoto 

Traction force microscopy is a simple, non-invasive method that can quantify cellular contact forces at the cell-substrate interface. It solves an inverse problem of determining the force field from measured substrate deformation. Because this problem is ill-posed with a large condition number, it is necessary to suppress the amplification of measurement noise during inversion. Previous studies have employed algorithms such as regularization or filtering that utilize spatial information to discriminate noise and true signals. Here, we propose an alternative approach that utilizes temporal information of the system. This method employs Kalman filter, a simple data assimilation algorithm in time series analysis, to recover the force field. Using numerically generated data, we show that the method is more accurate than standard algorithms including L2-regularization and is effective at filtering out temporal noise. Using experimental data on locomoting cells, we demonstrate that the method can reliably infer time-varying cellular traction forces. We also demonstrate two extensions of the proposed method: incorporation of additional knowledge and direct inference of low-dimensional force characteristics. These practical advantages will motivate the use of proposed framework for analyzing dynamic cell mechanics.

title: EIHR-PROT: explicit modelling of homology reliability for protein function prediction
abstract:
Background
                      Sequence-derived predictions and homology evidence provide complementary inputs for protein function annotation, but how their contributions should vary across proteins remains an open question. We investigated EIHR-PROT (Explicitly Incorporated Homology Reliability Signals for PROTein Function Prediction), which combines frozen ESM-2 embeddings, trainable attention pooling, and a neural prediction branch with DIAMOND-derived homology priors. A learned gate assigns protein-specific fusion weights using maximum bitscore, maximum query coverage, log-transformed retained-hit count, and hit availability. 
                  
                     Results
                      On Protein Data Bank (PDB) and low-homology AlphaFold (AF) test sets, EIHR-PROT achieved Fmax values of 0.604, 0.731, and 0.676 on PDB and 0.425, 0.507, and 0.564 on AF for biological process (BP), molecular function (MF), and cellular component (CC), respectively. These exceeded the evaluated naïve, DIAMOND Score, DeepGOPlus, and TALE+ baselines. Relative to sequence-conditioned gating, EIHR-PROT improved Fmax and area under the precision–recall curve and reduced minimum semantic distance for BP and MF on both datasets, with paired 95% bootstrap intervals excluding zero. It also improved PDB Fmax across all aspects relative to learned fixed fusion. However, advantages over fixed and identity-conditioned fusion varied by dataset and metric, with both alternatives remaining competitive on AF. Mean homology weights varied little across retained-hit identity bins, with the largest change occurring when no hits were retained. 
                  
                     Conclusion
                      EIHR-PROT supports reliability-conditioned sequence–homology fusion, with benefits clearest for BP and MF relative to sequence-conditioned gating. Its practical advantage over alternative fusion strategies depends on the dataset and evaluation objective. The implementation is available at github.com/uwidia/EIHR-PROT.

title: Soft-voting for robust common line assessment in cryo-EM angular reconstruction
abstract:
Background
                      Single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) reconstructs three-dimensional (3D) macromolecular structures from two-dimensional (2D) projection images acquired at unknown orientations. Common line-based angular reconstruction estimates projection orientations from pairwise common lines, but reliable common line detection remains challenging at the low signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs) typical of cryo-EM experiments. Existing voting-based approaches either assign equal weight to all votes or apply hard binary thresholds, thereby discarding valuable confidence information and limiting orientation estimation accuracy. 
                  
                     Results
                      We present Soft-Voting, a common line assessment framework that replaces binary vote weighting with continuous confidence weighting. For each projection pair, Soft-Voting constructs a consensus histogram of candidate dihedral angles using information from all remaining projections, with each vote weighted according to the reliability of its supporting common lines. The resulting common-line reliability scores are used to construct pairwise weights for spherical embedding, enabling globally consistent orientation recovery. Experiments on a synthetic dataset (EMD-33026) with SNRs ranging from 1 to 1/16 show that Soft-Voting generally achieves lower orientation errors than existing common line-based methods, especially under low-SNR conditions. Experiments on three real cryo-EM datasets (EMPIAR-10028, EMPIAR-10328, and EMPIAR-10455) further show that Soft-Voting produces competitive ab initio reconstructions based on Fourier shell correlation against reference maps. 
                  
                     Conclusions
                      The results indicate that Soft-Voting can improve common-line assessment and the robustness of cryo-EM angular reconstruction, particularly under challenging low-SNR conditions.

title: The SlHYL1‐SlRBP1 module integrates gibberellin metabolism to promote plant height in tomato (Solanum lycopersicum)
authors:
Xingxing Zhang, 
Miao Chai, 
Linjing Cao, 
Shengbo Chen, 
Kun Zhao, 
Jiazhen Han, 
Ning Li, 
Hongjiao Zhao, 
Shengjun Feng, 
Bo Wang, 
Shengze Zhang, 
Yumeng Li, 
Mingze Xu, 
Guodong Ren, 
Shuai Gao
abstract:
SUMMARY 
 Plant height is an essential agronomic trait that significantly influences crop yield and quality. The HYPONASTIC LEAVES 1 (HYL1), a core component of microRNA biogenesis, remains poorly understood in terms of its regulatory mechanisms on agronomic traits in tomato ( Solanum lycopersicum , Sl). In this study, we demonstrated that CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout of  SlHYL1  caused dwarfism, and partial suppression of  SlHYL1  in tomato cultivar “Ailsa Craig” (AC) via RNA interference (RNAi) increased internode number but reduced internode length, resulting in a semi-dwarf phenotype, confirming the role of SlHYL1 in regulating plant height. Cytological analysis showed that  SlHYL1  suppression decreased both cell number and size within internodes. Yeast two-hybrid screening identified that SlHYL1 interacted with another tomato RNA-binding protein 1 (SlRBP1). Knockdown of  SlRBP1  resembled the  SlHYL1-RNAi  semi-dwarf phenotype. Further studies revealed that the SlHYL1-SlRBP1 module additively promotes the expression of gibberellin (GA) biosynthetic genes, thereby facilitating GA accumulation. Additionally, the dwarf phenotypes of both  SlHYL1-RNAi  and  SlRBP1-RNAi  plants were partially rescued by exogenous GA 3  application. Notably, unlike SlHYL1, SlRBP1 did not affect the biogenesis of most miRNAs. In summary, our findings demonstrate that the SlHYL1-SlRBP1 module regulates tomato plant height by enhancing GA accumulation.

title: mRNA Decay Mediates Evolution and Biological Functions in Plant Gene Expression
authors:
Haidan Wu, 
Dayin Lv, 
Yelin Huang, 
Yuchi He
abstract:
ABSTRACT 
 mRNA decay is a key post-transcriptional regulatory mechanism that fine-tunes plant development and stress adaptation through dynamic mRNA stability control, bridging fundamental biology and crop improvement. Current knowledge of mRNA decay mechanisms in plants, largely derived from  Arabidopsis , is poorly generalisable across plant lineages owing to insufficient exploration of other species. Recent advances in high-throughput sequencing have accelerated the discovery of mRNA decay mechanisms. Here, we systematically illustrate its core molecular mechanisms alongside breakthrough advances. We further dissect evolutionary characteristics of highly conserved core components and lineage-specific adaptive variations across eukaryotes. Notably, conserved since the last eukaryotic common ancestor (LECA), this machinery reflects a complex ancestral eukaryote and provides high-resolution phylogenetic markers for reconstructing eukaryotic origins. We also clarify the essential biological roles of mRNA decay in developmental modulation and stress responses. Finally, we propose precision breeding strategies based on mRNA stability regulation to develop high-yielding, climate-resilient crops. This review integrates up-to-date mechanistic evidence and comparative evolutionary perspectives, consolidates consensus findings and sorts out inconsistent research outcomes, and seeks to enrich the fundamental biological understanding of plant mRNA stability modulation.

title: Aridity reshapes leaf and root trait dispersion through distinct microbial pathways
authors:
Man Hu, 
Xing Zhang, 
Hang Shi, 
Jie Gao, 
Rui He, 
Quanfa Zhang, 
Haishan Dang
abstract:
Piecewise structural equation model and decomposition of standardized effects.
 
 
 Summary 
 
Aridity is a primary driver of plant community assembly, yet most trait-based studies focus on mean traits rather than trait dispersion. Soil microbes may mediate plant responses to aridity, but whether leaf and root trait dispersion responds to aridity through shared or distinct microbial pathways remains unclear.
Using 535 species-by-plot records (247 species) along an aridity gradient in north-west China, we quantified four leaf and four root traits, soil properties, microbial diversity and composition, and microbial carbon use efficiency. We tested whether aridity differentially regulates leaf vs root functional dispersion (FD 
    is 
 ), and whether these responses are associated with different microbial predictors.
Leaf traits shifted more consistently with aridity and were more tightly linked to environmental variation than root traits. Leaf FD 
    is 
  negatively correlated with CUE, whereas root FD 
    is 
  negatively correlated with fungal diversity and bacterial community composition. These associations weakened toward less arid sites. Structural equation modeling further showed that leaf FD 
    is 
  linked primarily to microbial functioning, whereas root FD 
    is 
  linked more strongly to microbial diversity and composition.
Our results reveal that aridity reshapes trait dispersion through organ-specific plant–microbe pathways, highlighting that predicting dryland community responses to increasing drought must treat above- and belowground traits separately.

title: Aligning auxin supply to developmental demand in adventitious rooting
abstract:
The dose–time program of adventitious root (AR) formation.







Summary
Adventitious root (AR) formation is the developmental process that makes vegetative propagation possible, underpinning forestry, horticulture, and the clonal multiplication of elite and hard‐to‐propagate genotypes. Despite a detailed understanding of auxin's stage‐specific roles across the rooting program, propagation practice still treats auxin supply as a quantity to set rather than a profile to match. We argue that this produces a temporal mismatch between auxin supply and developmental demand: the available evidence shows that exogenous auxin availability frequently declines before the stages it should support are complete, particularly in slow‐to‐root and recalcitrant species, where developmental timelines are longest. New delivery tools, such as slow‐release conjugates, encapsulation systems, and selective auxin agonists, now make time‐structured delivery profiles feasible, but realizing their potential requires a different starting point. Rather than optimizing auxin dose empirically against rooting outcome, the field should characterize the spatiotemporal auxin demand curve across AR stages and design delivery profiles to match it. We outline the conceptual framework for this shift and the experimental approaches now available to support it.

title: Thermal acclimation as an emergent property of economically optimal photosynthesis
authors:
Wenyao Gan, 
Josef Garen, 
Sean T. Michaletz, 
I. Colin Prentice, 
Sandy P. Harrison
abstract:
Observed vs modelled relationships between (a)  T 
 opt  and growth temperature and (b) normalised  A 
 opt  and growth temperature for different species.
 
 
 Summary 
 
Leaf-level photosynthesis acclimates to growth conditions over days to weeks, with the instantaneous optimal temperature for photosynthesis ( T 
 opt ) increasing with growth temperature ( T 
 growth ). We investigated how this behaviour emerges in the P model, a primary production model based on eco-evolutionary optimality hypotheses.
We evaluated the P model estimates against experimental data for three herbaceous species grown at different temperatures and examined mechanisms underlying the responses of  T 
 opt  and the photosynthetic rate at  T 
 opt  ( A 
 opt ).
The model yields a realistic increase in  T 
 opt  with  T 
 growth  and a peaked relationship between  A 
 opt  and  T 
 growth . These responses emerge largely from adjustment of the stomatal sensitivity parameter ξ, which determines the internal-to-ambient CO 2  ratio ( c 
 i  :  c 
 a ) and its sensitivity to vapour pressure deficit. Rubisco kinetics ( K ) does not acclimate in the model, but its temperature dependence enters acclimation through optimality, mainly via ξ, shifting  T 
 opt . The decline in  A 
 opt  at high growth temperatures, often attributed to heat stress, reflects the narrowing gap between  T 
 opt  and  T 
 growth  because the  T 
 opt  shift has a slope below one.
The P model provides a mechanistic explanation for observed trends in  T 
 opt  and  A 
 opt  and a scalable approach for representing biochemical and stomatal acclimation in land-surface models.

title: Fruit color and size provide reliable signals of macronutritional rewards for seed dispersers
authors:
Boyu Lei,
