abstract:
Here, we reveal that fruit color and size traits signaled macronutrient reward specifically relating to bird‐, mammal‐, and mixed‐dispersed dispersal syndromes. Birds prioritize fruit color, while mammals prioritize fruit size to achieve optimal macronutritional reward, and these signal‐mutualist relationships are shaped by associated disperser traits, demonstrating co‐evolutionary mechanisms driving adaptive differentiation of fruit morphological and macronutrient traits. Our findings connect classical dispersal‐syndrome research with more recent developments in signal theory, trait‐matching theory, optimal foraging theory, and nutritional geometry theory, thus advancing the seed disperser mutualism paradigm.







Summary

Fruit color and size provide vital cues for determining seed dispersers' preferences; however, any consistent underlying link between these traits and fruit macronutritional rewards remains to be established by large‐scale analyses.
We collated a global database comprising 2626 observations of 1626 fruiting plant species from 460 global sites to test whether fruit color and size traits do indeed consistently signal macronutritional rewards to frugivores.
We found that consistent fruit color and size signaled macronutrient reward specifically relating to bird‐, mammal‐, and mixed‐dispersed dispersal syndromes. Lipids were the predominant macronutrient in black, blue, red, orange, and yellow fruits with birds (27.24%), whereas sugar predominated in mammal‐dispersed fruits (72.55%). Fruits dispersed by mammals (25.55 mm) were consistently larger than those dispersed by birds (10.17 mm) regardless of fruit color, and total macronutrient mass per fruit increased with fruit size. These signal‐mutualist relationships are shaped by associated disperser traits, demonstrating co‐evolutionary mechanisms driving adaptive differentiation of fruit morphological and macronutrient traits.
By integrating the disperser syndrome hypothesis and signal theory with nutritional geometry theory and trait‐matching theory, our study expounds the role of seed disperser selective preferences in the evolution of fruit traits, thus advancing the seed disperser mutualism paradigm.

title: Rice bZIP11 acts as a transcriptional repressor that negatively regulates photosynthesis in response to nitrogen deficiency
authors:
Namie Ohtsuki, 
Yasuhito Sakuraba, 
Mailun Yang, 
Yoshiaki Ueda, 
Shuichi Yanagisawa
abstract:
Phenotypes of 43-d-old wild-type (WT), Osbzip11-KO, and OsbZIP11-OX seedlings grown under control N and low N conditions.
 
 
 Summary 
 
Nitrogen (N)-deficiency responses, which are closely linked to plant biomass and crop yield, differ between plant tissues. A previous  in silico  analysis suggested that four transcription factors, including OsbZIP11, play vital roles in the gene regulatory network governing N-deficiency responses (NDRs) in rice roots.
To investigate the role of OsbZIP11 in NDRs, the phenotypes, functional responses, and gene expression of rice plants that either lacked functional OsbZIP11 or overexpressed  OsbZIP11  were analyzed.
Contrary to expectations, OsbZIP11 function showed an overwhelmingly stronger association with photosynthetic gene expression than with any other physiological process, including the expression control of N-related genes. OsbZIP11 directly suppressed numerous photosynthetic genes as a transcriptional repressor. N deficiency increased  OsbZIP11  expression in shoots, consistent with N deficiency-reduced photosynthetic activity. Furthermore, removing functional OsbZIP11 and  OsbZIP11  overexpression produced opposite effects on the expression of genes involved in the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis and carbon dioxide fixation, as well as on growth and grain yield.
These findings indicate that OsbZIP11 is a critical factor responsible for N deficiency-induced decreases in photosynthesis in rice and provide new insights into the mechanism underlying the coordination of C and N acquisition.
 
 まとめ 
 
植物のバイオマスや作物の収量と密接に関連する窒素(N)欠乏応答は、植物組織によって異なる。これまでに計算科学的手法により、OsbZIP11を含む4つの転写因子が、イネの根における窒素欠乏応答を制御する遺伝子調節ネットワークにおいて重要な役割を果たしていることが示唆されていた。
窒素欠乏応答におけるOsbZIP11の役割を解明するため、機能的なOsbZIP11を欠くイネおよび OsbZIP11 遺伝子を過剰発現させたイネの表現型、機能的応答、および遺伝子発現を解析した。
予想に反して、OsbZIP11の機能は、窒素関連遺伝子の発現制御を含む他のいかなる生理的プロセスよりも、光合成関連遺伝子の発現と圧倒的に強い関連性を示した。OsbZIP11は転写抑制因子として多数の光合成関連遺伝子の発現を直接的に抑制しており、また、窒素欠乏による光合成活性の低下と一致して、地上部における OsbZIP11 遺伝子の発現量は窒素欠乏により増加した。さらに、機能的なOsbZIP11の除去と OsbZIP11 遺伝子の過剰発現は、光合成の光依存反応や二酸化炭素固定に関与する遺伝子の発現、ならびに生育や穀粒収量に対して、正反対の影響をもたらした。
これらの知見は、OsbZIP11がイネにおける窒素欠乏による光合成低下を担う重要な転写因子であることを示しており、植物における炭素と窒素の獲得の協調的制御を司るメカニズムに関する新たな知見を提供するものである。

title: Rhg1-mediated selective autophagy degrades the nematode effector HgGID to increase soybean cyst nematode resistance
abstract: Abstract Plant-parasitic nematodes are sophisticated metazoan pathogens that deploy complex, animal-like effector repertoires to manipulate host cellular machinery. The  Rhg1  locus drives the primary resistance against soybean cyst nematode ( Heterodera glycines ), yet the mechanism by which its encoded atypical Soluble N-ethylmaleimide-sensitive factor Attachment Protein 18 (SNAP18) proteins restrict this evolutionarily advanced pathogen remains a long-standing enigma. Here, we reveal that  Rhg1 -mediated resistance operates as a suicide-bait strategy that converts a nematode virulence factor into a selective-autophagic trap. TurboID proximity labeling identified HgGID (glucose-induced degradation), a secreted nematode effector that physically associates with SNAP18 and co-enriches ubiquitin-proteasome components and SNARE-associated factors, consistent with a virulence strategy that engages host trafficking machinery during syncytium formation. Notably, the  Rhg1 -encoded atypical SNAP18 variant subverts this virulence strategy. We show that HgGID binds all 3 SNAP18 variants, whereas the resistance-associated SNAP18 LC/HC  variants favor increased dynamic accessibility of the HgGID AIM and promote its ATG8-dependent selective degradation. Ultimately, this targeted autophagic clearance efficiently neutralizes the virulence function of HgGID, establishing a novel paradigm for plant immunity against metazoan pathogens. Our findings uncover a molecular arms race where the host repurposes its vesicle transport machinery into an immune trap, highlighting the central role of selective autophagy in determining the outcome of host-metazoan interactions.

title: An Asynchronous Neuromorphic Architecture for Wearable EEG Emotion Recognition
abstract: Abstract Neural activity associated with emotion is event-driven and temporally sparse, whereas electroencephalography (EEG) is acquired as a continuous signal rather than a usable event stream. Conventional synchronous hardware processes all time steps densely, increasing energy costs during prolonged wearable monitoring. We propose an asynchronous neuromorphic architecture in which a dynamic adaptive spiking neural network converts features derived from EEG into sparse spike events. The model combines a depthwise separable gating module, division-free time-to-first-spike encoding, and adaptive temporal window regulation. The resulting events drive a globally asynchronous locally synchronous (GALS) accelerator that activates data movement and computation only for valid events, reducing switching during idle periods. DA-SNN outperforms lightweight models on SEED, SEED-IV, SEED-V, DEAP, and DREAMER. The accelerator completes inference on a preprocessed EEG tensor in 18 μs, with total power consumption of 148 mW and energy consumption of 2.66 μJ per inference.

authors: Kendra Sirak, Miguel Delgado, Angélica Viviana Triana Vega, Sebastián Rivas, Pedro Argüello, Ana María Boada, Javier Rivera-Sandoval, Germán Peña, Carl Langebaek, Juan Pablo Ospina, Sonia Archila, Saúl Alberto Torres Orjuela, Martha Beatriz Mejía Cano, Freddy Rodríguez Saza, Alison Barton, Kim Callan, Elizabeth Curtis, Trudi Frost, Lora Iliev, Aisling Kearns, Jack Kellogg, Ann Marie Lawson, Lijun Qiu, J. Noah Workman, Matthew Mah, Mariam Nawaz, Gregory Soos, Alexander Cherkinsky, Carla S. Hadden, Keith M. Prufer, Swapan Mallick, Nadin Rohland, Lars Fehren-Schmitz, David Reich
abstract: Ancient DNA data and stable isotope data from the eastern Colombian Andes reveal that C4-enriched resources were incorporated into local food webs during five millennia of genetic continuity and that a later population turnover introduced people with ancestry admixed between that found in Chibchan-related groups and that found at the Amazonian-Andean interface.

title: Fatty acid desaturation controls cellular fate decisions between senescence and ferroptosis
authors: Chisaka Kuehnemann, Samantha T. Jezak, Bronwyn A. Mogck, Niharika Kura, Rushmeen Tariq, Yuheng Che, Maija Vaittinen, Ioannis Siokas, Sharvari Deshpande, Carlyn Guthrie, Xuejuan Tan, Eliezer Aimontche, Aleksandra Aljakna Kahn, Peter Reifsnyder, Gung Lee, Amene Majidipur, Andrew H. Kung, Qiaoling Wang, Diana Jurk, Tong Zheng, Andrew S. Greenberg, Xiang-Dong Wang, Koji Kitazawa, Gregory Dolnikowsi, Yong Cheng, Nirupa R. Matthan, Arvind Ramanthan, Jennifer Lee, Daniel Roh, Howard H. Chen, Jussi Pihlajamaki, Ron Korstanje, Christopher D. Wiley
abstract: Polyunsaturated fatty acid metabolism shapes cell fate decisions: loss of DGLA favors senescence, whereas DGLA repletion triggers ferroptosis.

title: Pycea: a scverse toolkit for single-cell lineage tracing analysis
authors: Colgan, W. N., Weine, E., Koblan, L. W., Jones, M. G., Weissman, J. S., Yosef, N.
abstract: Lineage tracing enables reconstruction of cellular histories in development, regeneration, and disease, but integrating lineage data into single-cell analysis workflows remains challenging. We introduce Pycea, a Python toolkit for lineage analysis and visualization, and TreeData, an extension of AnnData that stores lineage trees alongside cellular measurements. TreeData is compatible with Scanpy and other scverse tools, enabling integrated analysis without converting between formats. Pycea provides scalable methods for tree visualization, clade identification, distance comparisons, ancestral state inference, and lineage statistics. This software is open source and available at https://github.com/YosefLab/pycea.

title: Single-cell perturbation prediction near experimental reproducibility with GENESIS
authors: Conci, R., D'Ascenzo, D., Cultrera di Montesano, S., Raghavan, S., Winter, P. S., Van Allen, E. M., Crawford, L., Lotter, W.
abstract: Single-cell perturbation atlases now measure cellular responses across millions of cells, but the number of possible combinations of biological contexts, perturbations, doses and other experimental variables make exhaustive measurements infeasible. Here, we present GENESIS (Generative ENErgy-based Single-cell Intervention Simulator), a generative framework that predicts single-cell response distributions directly from the covariates defining an experimental condition. GENESIS uses a lightweight neural network trained with the energy score, a strictly proper scoring rule for distributions. We introduce an experiment-calibrated evaluation framework in which prediction error is interpreted relative to the reproducibility of repeated measurements of the same condition. Across the Tahoe-100M small-molecule atlas and a large PBMC cytokine atlas, GENESIS significantly outperforms existing generative models and statistical baselines and approaches experimental reproducibility on independently repeated conditions. Importantly, GENESIS remains accurate when trained on only a fraction of the available experimental conditions or cells, and generated profiles recover experimentally observed context-dependent transcriptional programs. At comparable training-cell budgets, GENESIS achieves more accurate predictions when measurements span more experimental conditions rather than profiling fewer conditions more deeply. Together, these findings suggest a complementary strategy for perturbation studies: broader, lower-depth measurements can expand experimental coverage, while GENESIS augments sparsely sampled populations and predicts responses in unmeasured conditions.

title: Twenty-five new microsporidian genomes: Insights into ploidy, reproduction, and the group's pangenome
authors: Khalaf, A., Ayala, D., Bailey, N. W., Bote, L., Francis, O., Jaron, K. S., King, E., Lawniczak, M., Mullin, P., Powers, K., Powers, T., Santos, C., Blaxter, M.
abstract: Microsporidia are single-celled, obligately intracellular eukaryotic parasites of growing importance. Many aspects of their biology remain enigmatic, partly because of difficulties in sampling, culturing, and experimentally manipulating them. Here, we continue efforts to generate microsporidian genomes from serendipitously infected organisms sequenced for biodiversity genomics initiatives, such as the Darwin Tree of Life Project. We present 25 new microsporidian genomes: 14 biologically complete, including several at (near-)chromosome level, and 11 partial. Using RNA-seq data for three published genomes we identify Prokka as a suitable ab initio annotation approach for Microsporidia. Consistently annotating all available genomes, we investigate gene-content diversity across microsporidian clades. We find that the microsporidian pangenome exhibits extreme diversity, and that current genomic data substantially undersample the group's proteome space. Neither GC content nor genome span consistently explains orthogroup number across lineages, suggesting different evolutionary pressures. We find few one-to-one orthogroups in Microsporidia, as well as few orthogroups that are both lineage-specific and conserved across most species within a given lineage. Finally, Hi-C data confirm that tetraploid Amblyosporida microsporidia occur as two equivalent diploid units. In contrast, one Enterocytozoonida tetraploid genome suggests that all four genome copies occur within a single nucleus (a 'monokaryon'), confirming a previous proposal.

title: Differentiable Spin-Center Diffusion Model Enables DEER-Guided Generative Pipeline of Weighted Protein Ensembles
authors: Kao, T.-Y., Meiler, J., Mchaourab, H. S.
abstract: Biological function entails the interconversion of a protein between distinct conformations, an equilibrium modulated by ligands and other physicochemical conditions. Double electron-electron resonance (DEER) spectroscopy captures these ensembles as distance distributions, P(r), between spin label pairs. However, the width of P(r) convolves protein conformational heterogeneity with the rotameric flexibility of the label. Because current spin label models overestimate this contribution, translating P(r) into ensembles has remained indirect and predominantly qualitative. Here, we developed spin-center (SC) diffusion, a differentiable model of the spin label with a tunable spin label rotameric width. Coupled to a frozen Boltz-2 structure generator, SC diffusion enables the entire experimental P(r) to guide ensemble generation at inference time. We demonstrate the robustness of this pipeline on synthetic P(r) of known composition, recovering the ensemble populations, including both components of a bimodal profile. Guided by experimental P(r) measured under different biochemical conditions, ensembles of the transporters PfMATE, LmrP, MhsT and P-glycoprotein were modeled and free energy differences derived from the ensembles in a condition-dependent manner. By embedding a differentiable label model in structure generation, our approach interprets DEER distributions as weighted conformational ensembles, adding a missing thermodynamic grounding to generative protein structure prediction methods.

title: Gene Embedding Hub: a standardized resource for human gene representations
authors: Tabares, D., Bohl, M., Boeva, V.
abstract: Gene embeddings are vector representations of gene identity that provide machine-learning models with information from diverse biological sources. However, their use is hindered by a lack of standardization: inconsistent identifiers, formats, and preprocessing conventions. In this work, we present a unified resource of 67 human gene-embedding sets derived from protein, DNA and RNA sequences, biomedical text, bulk expression data, single-cell expression models, functional data, biological networks, knowledge graphs, regulatory genomics and multimodal models, covering up to 20,097 GENCODE-annotated protein-coding genes. The collection includes both published precomputed embeddings and representations generated or extracted from publicly available models and biological data. Each embedding set is organized in a folder containing the embedding matrix, the Ensembl gene identifiers, machine-readable metadata, and processing documentation. We validate the resource by measuring global and local similarity, cross-embedding consensus, and cross-embedding predictability. The collection is designed to allow community-contributed embeddings that meet predefined technical and documentation requirements, enables comparison of gene representations across modalities and provides standardized embeddings for training and downstream applications.

title: ScanFold3: a robust and rapid approach for identifying structured RNA targets in genomes and transcriptomes
authors: Coppenbarger, E., Dapour, A. O., Andrews, R. J., Moss, W.
abstract: Background. The rapid expansion of high-throughput transcriptomic datasets has created a critical need for scalable tools to identify functional RNA secondary structures. While thermodynamics-based folding is a well-established method, most algorithms lack the scalability required for genomic-scale datasets due to O(n3) time complexity. Methods. We present ScanFold3, an enhanced version of the ScanFold pipeline that optimizes the "Fold" step for modern computing needs. This version models consensus structure generation as a minimum perfect weighted matching problem on a graph. To ensure maximum scalability, we implemented a Greedy Approximation Algorithm and optimized performance-critical components in C++. Results. Benchmarking on sequences up to 128 kb demonstrates that ScanFold3 achieves a 38-fold to 129-fold increase in speed over ScanFold2. Validation against annotated human RNAs shows that ScanFold3 offers improved positive predictive value (PPV). Most significantly, when ScanFold3 outputs are used as structural constraints for global refolding, it outperforms previous versions across all metrics, including the F1 score. Conclusions. ScanFold3 provides a robust, speedy, and user-friendly method for characterizing the thermodynamics of novel RNA and DNA sequences. It is designed as an efficient first step for high throughput bioinformatic pipelines, capable of paring down chromosome-scale transcriptomic data into stable structures amenable to advanced analysis.

title: LIMBER: A Hybrid RNA Foundation Model for Predicting and Understanding RNA Structure and Function
authors: Wang, Z., Qiu, Y., He, Y., Thompson, I., Wang, H., Porter, A., Li, A.
abstract: RNA foundation models offer a promising route to decoding the relationships between RNA sequence, structure and function, yet how model shapes the acquisition and organization of biological information remains poorly understood. Here we introduce Layer-Interleaved Mamba-Bidirectional Encoder for RNA (LIMBER), a hybrid foundation model integrating bidirectional self-attention with selective state-space modeling, pretrained on 40.5 million non-coding RNA sequences. Through task-specific fine-tuning, LIMBER achieves leading performance on secondary-structure prediction and non-coding RNA classification benchmarks, while demonstrating strong transferability to translation-related tasks and RNA--small-molecule interaction prediction. Beyond model development, we establish a unified, task-agnostic framework to systematically evaluate and interpret the biological knowledge intrinsically acquired by RNA foundation models. This framework validates LIMBER's strong capabilities in recovering RNA structures and predicting mutational effects, while uncovering a hierarchical, task-dependent organization of different biological information across model layers. By further systematically training and evaluating a broad panel of model variants spanning model capacity, training duration and dataset size, we uncover distinct scaling behaviors across structural, evolutionary and functional capabilities. Together, these findings establish LIMBER as a versatile RNA foundation model and provide broader insights into how architectural design, internal representations and scaling shape the learning of RNA sequence-structure-function relationships.

title: Improving Molecular Docking Pose Recovery through Targeted Side-Chain Monte Carlo Sampling of an Apo Structure
abstract: Receptor flexibility complicates molecular docking when only an unbound (apo) protein structure is available. Local side-chain rearrangements can alter binding-pocket accessibility and ligand complementarity, motivating approaches that sample these motions efficiently. Here, we evaluate a targeted Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) protocol that combines local and larger side-chain torsional proposals with periodic molecular dynamics (MD) relaxation under harmonic backbone restraints. Receptor ensembles generated from an apo structure were evaluated against 859 experimental complexes from the OpenBind 2A protease benchmark and compared with the apo receptor and ensembles generated by restrained and unrestrained MD. With regular-space representative selection, MCMC recovered a ligand pose within 2 [A] of the experimental pose for 74.4% of complexes, compared with 51.0% for apo and 59.5% for restrained MD. Median minimum ligand heavy-atom RMSD decreased from 1.96 [A] for apo and 1.82 [A] for restrained MD to 1.62 [A] for MCMC. The largest gains occurred for complexes with greater side-chain displacement relative to pocket backbone displacement, consistent with the motions targeted by the protocol. MCMC representatives retained pocket geometries within the experimentally observed range, whereas unrestrained-MD representatives exhibited reduced pocket free volume and poor recovery. These findings support targeted side-chain sampling as a practical approach to generating apo-derived docking ensembles. The reported improvements measure best-case pose coverage across generated poses and receptors; their extension to prospective pose ranking and virtual screening remains to be established.

title: The Findings Workflow: An agentic, collaborative, provenance-tracked framework for scientific data analysis with Claude Code
authors: Riffle, M., Zelter, A., MacCoss, M. J.
abstract: Scientists presented with quantitative data often face two related problems: confidence that an analysis is statistically and computationally correct, and provenance sufficient to reproduce the resulting figures and conclusions. Large language models (LLMs) can make sophisticated analyses accessible through a collaborative, conversational interface, but unstructured use can worsen both problems by producing plausible but incorrect results and obscuring the steps that produced them. Here we present the Findings Workflow, a free, open-source Claude Code plugin designed to retain the flexibility of conversational LLM-assisted analysis while placing it within a structured, verifiable, and reproducible environment. The workflow uses staged, gated progression to ensure the science, metadata, and data are understood and tested data loaders are built before downstream analysis begins. Specialized subagents perform statistical analysis, programming, visualization, research, reporting, and validation, with independent review incorporated throughout. The plugin also provides vetted analysis templates, conventions, and methodological guidance that serve as trusted sources of opinion when deciding how analyses should be performed. Scientists remain actively involved throughout, exploring their data and directing the analysis through natural-language conversation, while the workflow supplies structure, verification, and persistent state around that collaboration. Findings are recorded automatically together with the data, code, methods, figures, and provenance needed to reproduce them. We demonstrate the workflow with a worked example that reproduces central findings from a published plasma extracellular vesicle proteomics dataset examining Alzheimer's disease (Mag-Net). Together, these features are designed to make LLM-assisted scientific analysis easier to trust, inspect, and reproduce without sacrificing its conversational and exploratory nature.

title: RNA assignment and segmentation geometry in Visium HD profiles of fibrostenotic Crohn's disease
abstract: Retrospective reuse of spatial transcriptomics often starts from a deposited bin-level Seurat object rather than the inputs needed to revisit upstream molecular processing. We tested whether image segmentation could support a defensible cell-like reconstruction under this constraint in two complete H&E-stained intestinal sections from a Visium HD study of Crohn's disease-associated fibrostenosis (GSE302569). The available data comprised 18,085 genes, 988,942 original 8 {micro}m bins and 179,596,575 UMIs. We evaluated 20 segmentation configurations in the preserved image coordinate system using a common bin-centre assignment rule, without restarting Space Ranger or introducing higher-resolution expression. RNA assignment ranged from 0% to 74.68% in CD1 and 0% to 64.05% in CD2. Expansion increased recovery but did not eliminate merged regions, straight boundaries or within-bin ambiguity; approximately 70-73% of InstanSeg brightfield nuclear regions received no assigned RNA. All 38 non-empty configuration-slice combinations underwent native full-mode RCTD against the same nine-group scIBD reference. Mean slice-level RNA recovery was negatively associated with primary-component dominance across 19 configurations (descriptive Spearman {rho} = -0.77). Neither dominant-call agreement nor concentrated RCTD support validates boundaries or cell identity. The observed limitations in RNA recovery, region geometry, and compositional support did not establish any tested configuration as a reliable single-cell reconstruction from these inputs. The findings identify limitations of retrospective single-cell reconstruction from the available binned inputs, not the impossibility of cell-resolved analysis from suitable original data.

title: Batch Effect Correction to Enhance Utility of a Publicly Available ALS Proteomics Dataset
authors: Cooper, G., Oh, I., Payne, P., Abrams, Z. R., Miller, T.
abstract: Large, publicly available databases of patient data have been successful in identifying associations between neurodegenerative diseases and biological features that might otherwise go unnoticed. The Answer ALS Consortium is one such database that has generated a rich repository of multi-omic data from people with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). However, large studies can suffer from batch effects that obscure genuine biological signal and prevent experiment reproducibility. In this study, we identified a batch effect in the Answer ALS 1-2 proteomic dataset (508 samples x 3,643 proteins) and corrected the effect using both the internal controls provided by Answer ALS and the batch effect-correction algorithm (BECA) ComBat. We identified a batch effect in the Answer ALS Dataset 1-2 proteomic dataset that, uncorrected, may obscure biology. Proteins MOS and H4 were outliers of expression in the dataset that correlated with the batch effect. Removing MOS and H4 did not correct the effect fully but did reveal new principal component (PC) contributing proteins related to motor neurons and potentially ALS: AINX, NFL, and NFM. The batch differential controls (BDCs) provided by Answer ALS were used to correct samples in their respective batches. ComBat, a well-characterized BECA, was applied to the dataset both before (ComBat-BDC) and after (BDC-ComBat) correction with the BDCs. BDC-ComBat was the only method that successfully reduced batch effect across the entire dataset. This method also preserved four of the top six PC-contributing proteins from the original dataset, including three neuronal proteins, suggesting that the corrected dataset recapitulates biology as well as the variability of the original dataset. Altogether, we produced a version of the Answer ALS proteomic dataset (354 samples by 3,641 proteins) with globally reduced batch effect and protein-level reduced batch effect. This version of the dataset recapitulates the individual protein variability and important neuronal proteins of the original. We also created a workflow for identifying and correcting batch effects that can be applied to other large data repositories.

title: Computational Repurposing of FDA Approved Drugs Against Cyclin Dependent Kinase (CDK2)
abstract: Drug repurposing is an approach for identifying new therapeutic with existing FDA approved drugs. Cyclin-dependent kinase 2 (CDK2) is an important regulator of cell cycle progression. The present study aimed to identify FDA-approved drugs with potential binding activity against CDK2 using a Computational drug-repurposing approach. The crystal structure of Human CDK2 (PDB ID: 3PY0) was used for Molecular docking, followed by Protein Ligand Interaction Profiler (PLIP) analysis to evaluate Protein Ligand interactions. Further for drug-likeness and pharmacokinetic properties using Swiss ADME and for Predicted toxicity using ProTox Was done. Based on this docking affinity, interaction profiles, drug-likeness, pharmacokinetics and toxicity, the best target was selected. Carteolol demonstrated the most balanced overall computational profile and was selected as the primary candidate for potential computational finding to provide repurposing against CDK2. Experimental studies are required to validate its direct binding and inhibitory activity against CDK2.

title: The Quagmire of Immunogenicity-Guided Antibody Design: Labels Limit Progress
authors: Villegas-Morcillo, A., Raman, C., Weber, J. M., Reinders, M. J. T.
abstract: Generative sequence-based antibody design is increasingly steered by learned property predictors, so a design objective is only as well specified as the labels behind its oracle. Immunogenicity is among the most clinically consequential properties to condition on, and among the least well specified: the supervisory signal is a single anti-drug-antibody percentage (ADA%) per molecule, aggregated from published trials. To analyze that signal, we first extended and corrected the widely used 217-entry dataset to 231 therapeutics with paired sequences, spanning formats from mouse to fully human. Then, we manually reconstructed the clinical evidence for 110 of them from primary sources. We find that an antibody format lookup outperforms every sequence-based learned predictor on the 231-antibody dataset. Apparent accuracy tracks the format composition of the evaluation split rather than sequence signal. Furthermore, the labels understate their own evidence: molecules labeled at [≤]6 ADA% span up to 86% across trials. We recomputed labels from the trial-level measurements and found that the advantage of the format-based approach disappears, while the sequence-based predictors degrade less under the cohort-weighted mean. We conclude that progress is limited by the label itself, and recommend reporting ADA% at the trial level, treating the target as a distribution rather than a point value, and evaluating against a format-based baseline.

title: FateDriver: Weakly supervised dual-view graph learning for transition-specific prioritization of candidate regulators in cellular reprogramming
authors: Sung, J., Son, K., Cha, H.-J., Kim, W., Lee, H.
abstract: Cellular reprogramming supports regenerative medicine, yet the endogenous regulators of a specified source-to-target transition remain incompletely defined. Existing computational methods rank candidate regulators from network topology, trajectory dynamics, or cell-state labels, leaving unused the factors experimentally delivered to induce the transition. We present FateDriver, a weakly supervised dual-view graph neural network that jointly represents cells and genes from single-cell transcriptomes, treats the delivered factors as sparse gene-level labels, and ranks the remaining genes for a specified transition under a positive--unlabeled formulation. Across two OSKM datasets and one GMT dataset, FateDriver ranked first or second among six methods in recovering externally curated reference genes, exceeded a supervision-matched non-graph model despite weaker co-expression with the delivered factors, and achieved the highest recovery of protein targets of pluripotency-inducing chemical cocktails in both OSKM datasets. Holding either the source or the endpoint fixed yielded distinct candidate programs, including a DDX58--interferon axis associated with cells lacking endogenous pluripotency markers. Applying the same framework to candidate source--target pairs prioritized distinct candidate origins for two in vivo partially reprogrammed intestinal populations. FateDriver converts sparse experimental knowledge into transition-specific hypotheses for regulator prioritization from single-cell trajectories.

title: Interpreting graph neural networks reveals microbial association patterns in inflammatory bowel diseases
authors: Cunha, A. F., Vidal, E., Barranco-Altirriba, M., Amigo, T., Assis, J. G., Nakaya, H. I., Santos, A.
abstract: Traditional machine learning models trained on gut microbiome abundance profiles can distinguish individuals with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) from non-IBD individuals. However, their interpretation typically considers taxa in isolation, making it difficult to understand how associations between taxa contribute to predictions. Here, we inferred individual-specific microbial association networks from longitudinal metagenomics data of 106 individuals in HMP2/iHMP and used them to train and interpret graph neural network (GNN) models, which we compared with abundance-based models such as Random Forest (RF). Although RF achieved higher predictive performance (AUPRC ~0.59 vs 0.446), interpreting the GNNs revealed that their predictions relied on a densely connected module of co-abundant Bacteroidales species. Unlike the taxa prioritized by RF, these species were not differentially abundant between conditions. In an independent cohort, this module carried most of the predictive signal, and removing its associations reduced performance to near chance. These results show that coordinated association structure, rather than abundance shifts alone, is a feature of the IBD gut microbiome, and that interpreting GNNs can uncover such patterns that complement abundance-based analyses.

title: Cross-modal transfer enables zero-shot prediction of drug responses across cell types
authors: Luo, C., Hu, M., Wu, Y., Guo, D., Wang, S., Lyu, Q. R., Liu, X.
abstract: Genetic perturbation responses capture the functional consequences of gene-level interventions, providing functional information for drug-response prediction beyond baseline gene expression. Within the same cellular context, genetic and chemical perturbations engage shared regulatory networks, providing a biological basis for transferring response information between perturbation modalities. Here we introduce GRAFT, a framework that combines genetic-to-chemical transfer with cross-context prediction to infer drug-induced transcriptional responses without drug measurements in the target context. Across benchmarked LINCS and external contexts, GRAFT improved response correlation, directional agreement and magnitude reconstruction over competing methods, particularly for drugs with context-dependent responses. GRAFT-Adapt further refines predictions of unmeasured responses using a small number of drug measurements from the target context. GRAFT-Atlas spans 13 cellular contexts and 7,856 drug catalog entries, comprising 102,128 predictions for drug-context combinations. The atlas captured recognizable pharmacological neighborhoods, shared functional programs, context-dependent transcriptional changes and structural-functional associations supported by molecular docking. Across ten iPSC lines from distinct donors, GRAFT identified candidate inter-donor differences, with functional support for selected candidates from measured genetic perturbation responses. Together, GRAFT enables perturbation-informed prediction and comparison of drug responses across cellular contexts.

title: Spatiotemporal modulation of microalgae to boost biofuel generation from CO 2  by the stick-to-culture strategy
abstract: Nature Communications, Published online: 01 November 2026;  doi:10.1038/s41467-026-79326-7  Balancing biomass growth and lipid accumulation remains a challenge in microalgal biofuel production. Here the authors report extracellular matrix-mimicking hydrogel scaffolds that dynamically reconfigure the microenvironment of spatially organized microalgae, allowing controlled switching between the two states.

title: The gene  ivory:mir-193  controls scale type differentiation in  Heliconius  butterflies
abstract: Nature Communications, Published online: 01 November 2026;  doi:10.1038/s41467-026-79315-w  Butterfly wing scales are diverse cell types that generate the colours and structures used in communication and adaptation. This study shows that the non-coding RNA ‘ivory’ controls alternative scale-cell states, linking regulatory evolution to phenotypic diversity.

title: Excess type I interferon disrupts developmental crosstalk and promotes premature distalization in trisomy 21 lungs
abstract: Nature Communications, Published online: 01 November 2026;  doi:10.1038/s41467-026-79210-4  Congenital lung anomalies are associated with Trisomy 21 lungs. Here, authors show that hyperactivation of the type I IFN signaling pathway promotes precocious epithelial cell differentiation, contributing to the T21 related lung pathologies.

title: Metabolic reprogramming modulates cardiomyocyte hypertrophy via GLS1 in chronic kidney disease in male mice
abstract: Nature Communications, Published online: 01 November 2026;  doi:10.1038/s41467-026-79129-w  Chronic kidney disease often causes heart enlargement, a serious complication whose mechanisms remain unclear. Here, the authors show that excess phosphate activates the metabolic enzyme GLS1, promoting heart enlargement, while blocking GLS1 protects against this effect in male mice.

title: When are Two‐Dimensional Covalent Organic Frameworks Good Electrodes for Lithium Ion Batteries? A Data‐Driven Analysis
authors:
Preeti Bhauriyal, 
Shubhajit Das, 
Thomas Heine
abstract:
A data-driven framework integrating density-functional theory with machine learning models screens two-dimensional covalent organic frameworks (2D COFs) from CoRE COF database to reveal atomic-level design rules: N/O-rich coordination pockets drive cathode behavior, while separated redox sites and π-rich galleries enable anode function in Li-ion batteries. Strategic pairing of 2D COFs as anode|cathode has the potential for an all-organic lithium battery architecture.

 
 
 ABSTRACT 
 Two-dimensional covalent organic frameworks (2D COFs) are emerging as sustainable organic electrode candidates for lithium-ion batteries. Despite more than a decade of research, existing heuristics for designing electroactive COFs lack generality, and the suitability of these materials as alternatives to conventional electrodes remains poorly resolved. Here, we map structure–electrode–function relationships across 1099 experimentally synthesized 2D COFs from the CoRE COF database by developing a data-driven framework integrating density-functional theory computations with machine learning models and establishing atomic-level design rules governing electrode behavior. We uncover that cathode-like character originates from dense, multidentate nitrogen and oxygen rich coordination pockets at pore walls, characteristic of imide, acylhydrazones, keto–amine linkages, and π-macrocycles, whereas anode-like behavior is encoded by spatially separated redox sites and π-rich interlayer galleries that sustain weak, reversible Li +  intercalation. Sequential voltage, capacity, and conductivity-based screening across the database yields 14 anode and 14 cathode candidates. We show that the known chemical space of 2D COFs cannot outperform inorganic electrodes in terms of operating voltages. However, strategic pairing of 2D anode|cathode pairs within an all-organic lithium battery architecture delivers full-cell voltages exceeding 2 V with capacities above 200 mAh g −1  on both electrodes, surpassing small organic molecules and polymer counterparts.

title: Early‐Life Polyethylene Microplastic Exposure Exacerbates ADHD‐Like Behaviors in Mice via PI3K/AKT1/Nrf2 Signaling: Evidence From the Pilot Cohort and Multi‐Omics Analyses
authors:
Yufan Luo, 
Ruijin Xie, 
Hua Xu, 
Xue Xiao, 
Wei Xiao, 
Qiyang Pan, 
Shengjie Xu, 
Li Liu, 
Zeliang Xiao, 
Yue Zhou, 
Chenyu Sun, 
Yu Wu, 
Yueying Liu
abstract:
Circulating polyethylene microplastic burden is positively associated with heightened ADHD symptom severity and systemic redox‐inflammatory imbalance in children. Mechanistic investigation in a developmental co‐exposure mouse model further demonstrates that microplastics aggravate ADHD‐like behaviors, dopaminergic dysregulation, and oxidative hippocampal injury. PI3K/AKT1/Nrf2 signaling is identified as a central mechanistic nexus linking microplastic‐induced neurotoxicity to neurodevelopmental vulnerability. Pharmacological modulation with melatonin partially restores pathway activity and ameliorates neurobehavioral deficits, establishing a modifiable therapeutic target for mitigating microplastic‐related developmental neurotoxicity. These findings integrate clinical association with experimental causation, supporting microplastic exposure as an emerging environmental risk factor for ADHD pathogenesis.








ABSTRACT
Microplastic pollution may influence neurodevelopment, yet its relationship with attention‐deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) remains unclear. We integrated a pediatric cohort, multi‐omics analyses, network toxicology, and animal experiments to investigate polyethylene (PE) microplastic exposure in ADHD vulnerability. Among 90 children, PE was the predominant polymer detected in blood and was more abundant in children with ADHD. Higher PE burden was associated with greater symptom severity, increased IL‐6, and reduced antioxidant capacity. Multi‐omics and network analyses converged on PI3K/AKT1/Nrf2 signaling. In a perinatal nicotine mouse model, developmental PE co‐exposure exacerbated ADHD‐like behaviors, dopaminergic dysfunction, and oxidative injury. Melatonin partially alleviated these abnormalities by restoring PI3K/AKT1/GSK3β and Nrf2 signaling, whereas AAV‐mediated PI3K knockdown weakened its protective effects. Collectively, the human findings identify circulating PE burden as an environmental correlate of ADHD‐related neurodevelopmental vulnerability, while the animal experiments provide evidence that developmental PE co‐exposure can aggravate ADHD‐like abnormalities in a susceptible background.

title: A CT Lesion Foundation Model for Non‐Invasive Assessment of Hepatocellular Carcinoma Aggressiveness and Prediction of Recurrence Risk
authors:
Wei Xia, 
Zhehan Shen, 
Mengsi Li, 
Jianxin Lu, 
Ji Xia, 
Yang Cheng, 
Wenzheng Li, 
Shunjie Dong, 
Lin Deng, 
Ruokun Li
abstract:
A computed tomography lesion foundation model, built by sequential self‐supervised pretraining on generic and hepatocellular carcinoma‐specific lesion images, non‐invasively assesses microvascular invasion and pathological grade from contrast‐enhanced CT and stratifies postoperative recurrence risk. Multicenter validation demonstrates robust performance, and imaging‐genomic analysis links high‐risk phenotypes to suppressed lymphocyte‐mediated immune programs.








ABSTRACT
Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains a leading cause of cancer‐related mortality worldwide, with high recurrence rates following curative resection. Accurate non‐invasive assessment of tumor aggressiveness and recurrence risk is critical for surgical decision‐making and postoperative surveillance, yet remains challenging with conventional imaging modalities. Here, we developed a CT lesion foundation model (LFM), trained via self‐supervised learning on 32,120 generic lesion and 6,387 HCC‐specific CT patches to capture transferable intra‐lesional imaging phenotypes. Across one internal and two external validation cohorts, the sequentially pretrained LFM (LFM‐Seq) achieved area under the curve values of 0.916, 0.846, and 0.920 for microvascular invasion (MVI) assessment, and 0.833, 0.885 and 0.795 for pathological grade assessment. The model remained robust under scenarios of limited training data and tumor localization perturbations. Furthermore, LFM‐Seq‐derived risk scores stratified recurrence‐free survival (RFS), yielding an externally validated C‐index of 0.701, and remained independently associated with RFS after adjusting for clinicopathological factors. Exploratory biological interpretability analyses showed that LFM‐Seq‐derived risk phenotypes were associated with suppressed lymphocyte‐related immune programs. These results suggest that CT lesion foundation models can support non‐invasive and robust characterization of HCC aggressiveness, recurrence risk stratification and discovery of interpretable prognostic imaging biomarkers.

title: Membrane‐Targeted Nanoparticles for Neuronal Photomodulation
authors:
Ane Escobar, 
Ana Sánchez‐Iglesias, 
Davide Bello, 
Miriam Feijoo Barriga, 
Alex M. Ascensión, 
Laura Rodríguez‐Gómez, 
David Otaegui‐Bichot, 
Francisco Javier Gil‐Bea, 
Monica Carril, 
Marek Grzelczak
abstract:
Immobilizing gold nanoparticles on the neural interface using a bioorthogonal approach generates localized heat upon exposure to near‐infrared light, temporarily inhibiting primary neuronal activity without damaging the cells. This precise placement and retention of nanoparticles at the cell membrane expand the strategies for non‐invasive neural network modulation.








ABSTRACT
Selective targeting of nanoparticles to the neuronal interface is central for the tailored development of precision neurotechnologies. Here, we report the targeting of gold bipyramids, as a model nanomaterial, on the membrane of primary neurons using a bioorthogonal approach. In a two‐step process, linker molecules anchor to receptors that expose trans‐cyclooctene, which forms a covalent bond with the tetrazine functional group on nanoparticles, leading to the retention of hundreds of nanoparticles per cell. Selective labeling of neuronal membranes with plasmonic nanoparticles via a bioorthogonal strategy enabled inhibition of neuronal activity through photothermal effects under NIR laser irradiation in synchronized cell cultures. The linker and/or nanoparticles alone have a negligible effect on neuromodulation. Nanoparticle retention at the membrane is rapid, requiring only one hour of total incubation, with no cytotoxic effect. These results expand the repertoire of light‐activated nanomaterials for non‐invasive neuromodulation.

title: Neutron Depth Profiling: The Core Link Connecting the Microscopic Mechanisms of Lithium‐Ion Batteries With Intelligent Design
authors:
Yulong Zhang, 
Chunjing Yue, 
Shijiao Liu, 
Muyang Chen, 
Xiaokang Shi, 
Rui Tan, 
Hongqing Hao, 
Jie Yang, 
Xinhua Liu
abstract:
Neutron depth profiling exploits the  6 Li(n, 3 H) 4 He reaction to provide quantitative, isotope-specific, depth-resolved maps of lithium inside operating lithium-ion batteries, directly linking lithium transport, dendrite growth and interfacial short-circuiting to a physics-informed machine-learning roadmap that turns this non-destructive operando measurement into a basis for intelligent battery design.

 
 
 ABSTRACT 
 Neutron Depth Profiling (NDP) is a non-destructive, in situ quantitative depth-analysis technique underpinned by neutron-induced nuclear reactions. Offering high  6 Li-isotope sensitivity and nanometer-to-micrometer depth resolution, NDP delivers isotope-resolved lithium spatial information hardly accessible via conventional probes including secondary-ion mass spectrometry (SIMS), X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), and operando neutron imaging, yet it suffers from depth-dependent resolution degradation, limited lateral performance, and requires large-scale neutron-beam facilities. This paper systematically reviews NDP fundamentals, global neutron-source progress, and cutting-edge battery applications, covering lithium-ion migration in electrodes, lithium dendrite nucleation and growth, and the “reversible short-circuit” effect at solid-electrolyte interfaces. The unique merit of NDP for quantitative  6 Li depth-profiling is highlighted, while noting that NDP cannot independently resolve full-element maps or nanoscale interfaces and demands complementary characterizations. A roadmap integrating NDP with multimodal measurements and physics-informed machine learning for intelligent battery design is outlined, alongside open challenges: inversion non-uniqueness under low-signal conditions and translation from model cells to practical batteries. This work provides actionable guidelines to leverage NDP for bridging microscopic lithium mechanisms and rational design of next‑generation batteries with high safety and high energy density.

title:
Natural variation in the evolutionarily conserved F‐box gene
                     SDEF 
                    promotes seed dormancy in rice
authors:
Yuliang Zhou, 
Yueping Wang, 
Guangmiao Zhao, 
Chunbao Liu, 
Ruizhen Zeng, 
Wenxuan Liang, 
Ru Han, 
Hui Kong, 
Xiaofan Cao, 
Minshi Li, 
Huhui Chen, 
Bin Tan, 
Hong Liu, 
Zhenjiang Xu
abstract:
SUMMARY 
                   
                    Insufficient seed dormancy causes pre‐harvest sprouting (PHS) and severe yield losses in rice; however, genetic resources with practical breeding value remain limited. Here, we isolated a major dormancy gene,
                     SDEF 
                    , via map‐based cloning using chromosomal single segment substitution lines (SSSLs), identifying a functional SNP (Arg‐to‐Trp) as the causal mutation. CRISPR/Cas9‐mediated knockout of
                     SDEF 
                    led to PHS susceptibility, while overexpression significantly enhanced dormancy. Importantly,
                     SDEF 
                    enhanced seed dormancy without compromising grain yield in SSSLs, confirming it as a promising breeding target. Moreover,
                     SDEF 
                    encodes an angiosperm‐conserved, nuclear‐localized F‐box protein and is preferentially expressed in the embryo, with expression increasing during seed maturation and declining upon germination. Mechanistically, protein interaction assays confirmed that SDEF recruits OSK1, with the Trp‐type SDEF
                     K 
                    exhibiting a more stable interaction than the Arg‐type SDEF
                     H 
                    .
                     SDEF 
                    is induced by abscisic acid (ABA) and appears to promote seed dormancy through the ABA pathway by activating ABA signaling genes and repressing α‐amylase genes, as evidenced by the reduced ABA sensitivity of
                     sdef 
                    mutants. Additionally, haplotype analysis revealed that natural variation in
                     SDEF 
                    is associated with divergent dormancy levels, and reduced nucleotide diversity in cultivated rice indicates that
                     SDEF 
                    was selected during domestication. Collectively, our results provide insights into the molecular basis of
                     SDEF‐ 
                    mediated dormancy, providing an ideal target for breeding PHS‐resistant rice.

title:
OsYchF1 
                    suppresses
                     OsEF1Bγ 
                    ‐mediated
                     ER 
                    detoxification to co‐involve the growth‐maintenance trade‐off in rice
authors:
Liyang Gao, 
Lulu Yu, 
Dongyu Chen, 
Rongfang Li, 
Yuhe Wang, 
Yunchuan Liao, 
Yetao Meng, 
Qian Li, 
Ying Miao, 
Gefei Hao, 
Rui Miao
abstract:
SUMMARY 
                   
                    Translation elongation is a fundamental biological process, yet its direct role in stress adaptation remains unclear. In this study, we uncover a novel regulatory axis in rice involving the unconventional G protein OsYchF1, which gates the detoxification activity of the elongation factor 1Bγ (OsEF1Bγ) in the endoplasmic reticulum. OsEF1Bγ is a subunit of the eEF1B complex and possesses an N‐terminal glutathione S‐transferase (GST) domain. We demonstrate that overexpression of OsEF1Bγ enhances rice tolerance to osmotic and saline stress by lowering malondialdehyde levels, suggesting its role as a positive regulator
                     via 
                    GST‐mediated detoxification. Conversely, we found that OsYchF1 interacts with OsEF1Bγ across multiple domains. This interaction competitively inhibits the binding of reduced glutathione to OsEF1Bγ by approximately 40‐fold, thereby suppressing its GST activity
                     in vitro 
                    . Consistently,
                     OsYchF1 
                    knockout mutants phenocopy OsEF1Bγ overexpressors, displaying enhanced stress tolerance, reduced reactive oxygen species accumulation, and increased antioxidant enzyme activities. Furthermore, we show that stress‐induced downregulation of OsYchF1 acts as a physiological trigger, releasing this molecular brake to enable rapid activation of OsEF1Bγ‐mediated detoxification in response to challenging environments. Collectively, our findings reveal a post‐translational mechanism where OsYchF1 serves as a molecular brake on the ER‐localized detoxification engine of OsEF1Bγ, fine‐tuning abiotic stress adaptation and establishing an unexpected link between the translation machinery and cellular redox homeostasis.

Mark A. Ratner (1942–2026): Founded molecular electronics while spearheading the growth of science at Northwestern University
abstract: Recently, we lost one of the original developers of the field of molecular electronics. Mark A. Ratner wrote a famous paper in 1974 that developed the theoretical framework for making a molecule act as a rectifier. This idea, and a host of further ideas that were stimulated by this and other papers, led to a huge amount of experimental and theoretical studies that continue to this day. But Mark’s career was much more than that, with leadership at Northwestern University and beyond that continues to shape the scientific enterprise.

Deep mutational scanning of the GPCR rhodopsin reveals pleiotropic mutational effects and their roles in modulating receptor signaling
abstract: Biophysical pleiotropy, the phenomenon in which a mutation affects multiple protein properties, underlies many genetic diseases and shapes protein evolution, yet remains poorly understood, limiting synthetic biology and therapeutic development. Although extensively studied in soluble proteins, little is known about how pleiotropic effects shaped the evolution of receptor protein functions. Here, we developed a cell-based assay designed to assess pleiotropic effects in G protein–coupled receptors (GPCRs), the largest receptor class in eukaryotes. Because our assay allows for multiple GPCR molecular phenotypes (basal activity, ligand-dependent signaling, and cellular receptor abundance) to be simultaneously assessed, we applied it to study rhodopsin, a visual GPCR that evolved for high phototransduction capabilities by maximizing light-driven responses while minimizing noise. To investigate this, we integrated our assay with deep mutational scanning to test the impacts of ~2,000 single-residue substitutions in rhodopsin across all three molecular phenotypes (~6,000 measurements). By analyzing these data in the context of rhodopsin’s protein structures, we found complex pleiotropic effects that act asymmetrically to impose joint constraints, restricting mutational tolerance in rhodopsin’s retinal binding pocket and G protein interaction interface. A dose–response analysis of rhodopsin signaling revealed that these pleiotropic constraints arise from the dual functions of its chromophore, which acts as an agonist upon light-driven isomerization but also an inverse agonist in darkness. Because these constraints reflect mechanistically driven limitations in the evolution of receptor signaling, these findings reveal a role for biophysical pleiotropy in shaping the signaling capabilities of receptor proteins.

title: Structural basis of glycoprotein recognition by the human folding sensor UDP-glucose:glycoprotein glucosyltransferase
abstract: UDP-glucose:glycoprotein glucosyltransferase 1 (UGGT1) plays a central role in quality control of glycoprotein folding within the early secretory pathway, yet the molecular basis of UGGT1 substrate recognition remains poorly understood. Here, we report cryo-EM structures of human full-length multidomain UGGT1. Monomeric UGGT1 structures reveal two conformational states corresponding to “open” and “closed” architectures. Three-dimensional variability and molecular dynamics simulations suggest the existence of intermediate conformations, leading to a model in which a continuum of structural transitions underlies UGGT1 function. Notably, in the open state, the EM-maps reveal at the top of the U-shaped protein a density that bridges the sensory TRXL2 and the glucosyltransferase catalytic domains, consistent with substrate association. This observation supports a mode of binding that places the substrate near the catalytic domain. A dimeric form of UGGT1 was observed in which the glycoprotein substrate binding sites are occluded, suggesting that dimerization may regulate UGGT1 activity. To better understand the spatial relationship between the site of misfolding and that of UGGT-mediated N-glycan reglucosylation, we identified N-glycosylation sites on endogenous glycoprotein substrates by glycoproteomics. No consensus sequence was found flanking modified sites, indicating that substrate recognition relies on mechanisms beyond primary sequence. Mutations in the UGGT1 gene cause a novel congenital disorder of glycosylation characterized by developmental delay and intellectual disability, and the human UGGT1 structure helps explain how disease-associated missense and deletion variants disrupt function. Together, our data provide insight into the relationship between UGGT1 structure and function, integrating enzyme conformational states with client glycoprotein interaction and processing.

title: In-context learning as a retraining-free paradigm for constitutive modeling
abstract: Constitutive modeling is fundamental to computational solid mechanics, yet most existing approaches remain material-specific and require retraining or recalibration when materials change. Here we introduce In-Context Modeling (ICM), a retraining-free paradigm for constitutive modeling that infers constitutive behavior from physical context rather than material-specific optimization. Using hyperelasticity as a testbed, we demonstrate that ICM can be trained once on equilibrium deformation fields spanning diverse materials, geometries, and boundary conditions, enforcing physical equilibrium without stress labels. After training, the same model can be directly deployed on previously unseen hyperelastic materials without retraining. At inference, ICM treats a small set of nonuniform strain fields as physical context to generate constitutive response in a single forward pass. Numerical benchmarks and experimental validation demonstrate accurate stress prediction across out-of-distribution materials and boundary-value problems, together with substantial reductions in deployment cost compared with per-material learning approaches. These results establish in-context learning as a retraining-free paradigm for constitutive modeling, particularly valuable for heterogeneous biological tissues such as the brain, and suggest a pathway toward foundation models for computational mechanics.

title: HAR1 receptor kinase links nodule autoregulation with repression of auxin signaling and lateral root development
abstract:
Nitrogen-fixing root nodules develop as lateral organs on legume roots and their formation is restricted by autoregulation of nodulation (AON), a systemic mechanism with unclear evolutionary origins. We identify
                     Lotus japonicus NUCLEAR FACTOR Y 
                    subunit
                     A4 
                    (
                     NF-YA4 
                    ) gene as a central target of the leucine-rich repeat receptor kinase HAR1, which controls both AON and root system architecture. Under nonsymbiotic conditions, HAR1 suppresses expression of
                     NF-YA4 
                    and its close paralog
                     NF-YA1 
                    , at least in part through a miR169-dependent mechanism, mirroring the
                     Arabidopsis 
                    CLAVATA1/2-miR169-
                     NF-YA 
                    module. Loss of
                     HAR1 
                    leads to
                     NF-YA4 
                    overexpression, broad transcriptional reprogramming, and induction of
                     LATERAL ORGAN BOUNDARIES DOMAIN 
                    ,
                     STYLISH 
                    , and
                     YUCCA 
                    auxin biosynthesis genes, enhancing auxin signaling and lateral root development. Grafting experiments show that
                     HAR1 
                    constrains
                     NF-YA4 
                    -mediated branching both locally in roots and systemically from shoots. Because
                     NF-YA4 
                    functions partly redundantly with
                     NF-YA1 
                    to mediate nodule emergence, our results suggest a model in which duplication and neofunctionalization of an ancestral NF-YA-dependent pathway controlling lateral root development facilitated its recruitment to the nodulation program. They also raise the possibility that AON could have evolved, at least in part, through the co-option of a LRR-RK/miR169/
                     NF-YA 
                    regulatory module that limited lateral root development.

title: Reply to Zhou and Tsao: Synergy rarely underlies the benefits of combination cancer therapy
Multiscale Brownian dynamics simulations reveal effects of macromolecular crowding on protein–ligand association
abstract: Macromolecular crowding is known to influence the diffusive, binding, kinetic, and equilibrium properties of proteins in a range of environments such as occur inside biological cells or in highly concentrated solutions of protein therapeutics. However a quantitative understanding of the effects of macromolecular crowding on the rates of protein-small molecule binding is lacking. Here, we present an adaptive model to simulate the association of two solutes in a macromolecularly crowded environment using Brownian dynamics and to compute the corresponding bimolecular association rate constant. The adaptive model represents interactions with atomistic detail for short-range crowder–noncrowder interactions, while using a coarse-grained approach for long-range crowder–noncrowder interactions and all crowder–crowder interactions. This multiscale approach is integrated in the Simulation of Diffusional Association (SDA) software for Brownian dynamics simulation of biomolecular diffusion. We applied this model to compute the rates of association for two contrasting protein-small molecule inhibitor complexes in environments varying in macromolecular crowder type and density, and we used Markov State modeling of the encounter trajectories to analyze the binding pathways. The results reveal competing effects: While the presence of the crowders can hinder ligand binding by reducing the translational diffusion rates of the solutes and obstructing the protein binding sites, crowders can also enhance the bimolecular association rate by other mechanisms, including channeling and the caging effect.

title: Origami state machine with time-varying magnetic fields
abstract: Achieving reliable, remote control over multiple stable states in modular systems remains a challenge due to the coupling between modules and history-dependent transitions. Here, we present magnetic origami state machines that enable deterministic navigation from any unknown initial state to any target state under magnetic actuation. By assuming mutually distinct energy barriers in modular Kresling origami assemblies, we realize fully accessible transition graphs with scalable state spaces. Guided by the graph associated to the state machine, a rotating magnetic field induces a universal reset that autonomously drives the system to a known equilibrium state from arbitrary states without sensing or feedback, while pulsed magnetic inputs further enable programmable transitions to any target state via prescribed actuation sequences. A reduced-order Lagrangian mechanics model predicts snap-through dynamics across reset, stepwise programming (between graph nodes), and shortcuts (by adapting pulse magnitude and orientation) where inertia triggers simultaneous multicell transitions with a single pulse. These results establish a general framework for programmable magneto-mechanical state machines with autonomous state reset and full state-space control.

title: AR signaling context and the apparent lack of synergy between AR-targeted therapy and PARP inhibition
Mechanism of catalytic regulation by an allosteric hot spot in dihydrofolate reductase
abstract: Allostery is central to catalysis and regulation, yet how distal perturbations control enzyme activity remains unresolved. Here we elucidate how a distal allosteric hot spot regulates catalysis in dihydrofolate reductase, a benchmark enzyme exhibiting latent allostery. We combine enhanced conformational sampling, reactive free-energy calculations of the chemical step, and perturbation-induced nonequilibrium molecular dynamics with evolutionary analysis and experimental kinetics to obtain a comprehensive molecular description of conformational landscapes, catalytic activity, and allosteric communication. We show that a mutational perturbation at the hot spot redistributes the populations of two globally similar conformations with a subtle but critical structural difference that makes one catalytically competent and the other not. Nonequilibrium relaxation simulations further reveal that the transition between these two states in the mutant proceeds through a stepwise sequence of local structural rearrangements rather than a concerted global motion. Guided by this mechanism, we rationally engineer a compensatory second-site mutation that partially restores activity. These results provide a unified thermodynamic and kinetic view of allostery and establish a general, mechanistically guided framework for engineering allosteric regulation in enzymes.

title: Where intention goes, responsibility flows: Grounding AI accountability in the machine learning paradigm
abstract: An opening salvo of lawsuits in US courts has begun holding AI companies accountable through independent doctrinal routes: Product liability and agency law cut as swords, while the shields of Section 230 immunity and First Amendment doctrine begin to crack. This Perspective points out that these converging paths share a unifying principle, built on the very engineering architecture of machine learning (ML) itself. Every ML system, across all variants, is constituted by a human-specified objective function before learning begins. Training data, deployment context, user interaction, and postdeployment oversight add further layers of deliberate human intention traceable to identifiable actors. AI output is therefore not the expression of a single speaker but a composite of layered human intents. It takes a village to raise an AI, and everyone in that village bears a duty of care. This transforms AI accountability from a philosophical puzzle into a tractable legal inquiry: Trace the chain of intentional design decisions across the ML pipeline, grade each actor’s responsibility by their intent’s specificity and foreseeability, and apportion liability accordingly, following the standard three doctrine-neutral questions (attribution, causation, apportionment). Sufficient for most cases, four gaps remain: who owes what share when many hands build one system, proving fault inside an opaque model, harms that surface only after deployment, and remedies that match the technology’s pace. Targeted reforms drawing on environmental, vaccine, and financial regulatory precedents can close these gaps without requiring new legal categories, AI speech rights, AI legal personhood, or defining AI consciousness.

title: Deciphering the molecular basis of maize cold tolerance via integrative regulatory network analysis
authors:
Tianshuo Li, 
Wei Wang, 
Chuang Jiang, 
Jinkui Cheng, 
Fei Yi, 
Liusheng Duan
abstract:
SUMMARY 
                   
                    Maize (
                     Zea mays 
                    L.) is a globally critical but cold‐sensitive crop. Understanding the temporal organization of cold‐responsive, circadian‐associated, and hormone‐associated transcriptional programs is essential for deciphering how plants balance growth and survival under cold stress to ensure food security. We performed high‐resolution time‐series RNA‐seq on 108 maize seedling samples across 14 time points (0–36 h cold stress and 24 h recovery). Coronatine (COR) was utilized as a defined JA‐associated chemical perturbation to probe hormone‐associated transcriptional responses during cold stress. We identified 12 986 cold‐responsive and 2259 recovery‐responsive genes, revealing a recovery‐associated transcriptional transition characterized by suppressed photosynthesis‐related processes and enrichment of genes associated with lipid catabolism, accompanied by transient physiological stress during early recovery. Cold stress induced widespread phase shifts and reduced oscillation amplitudes among circadian‐associated transcripts, while COR identified distinct hormone‐associated transcriptional modules and candidate network‐associated genes, including
                     ZmWRKY71 
                    and
                     ZmHSP28 
                    , whose roles were further supported by molecular and genetic analyses. This study establishes a temporally resolved transcriptional framework for maize cold stress and recovery, integrating transcriptional dynamics, physiological responses, and experimentally supported regulatory nodes.

abstract:
SUMMARY 
                   
                    Alfalfa (
                     Medicago sativa 
                    ), an autotetraploid species, is a globally important forage crop. Traditional genetic transformation methods predominantly rely on leaf‐derived callus, a process that is complex, inefficient, and particularly challenging to generate stable transgenic lines in polyploid plants. To address these limitations, we developed an efficient transformation system that bypasses callus induction by directly exploiting stem regeneration. Our protocol enables the generation of stable gene‐edited alfalfa plants from shoot tips. It accommodates stem explants from various developmental stages and significantly reduces the time required. Moreover, this approach was effective across multiple alfalfa cultivars, and preliminary proof‐of‐concept experiments in
                     Nicotiana tabacum 
                    and
                     Solanum lycopersicum 
                    suggested potential transferability beyond alfalfa. This study represents a substantial advancement in perennial plant transformation and provides a robust and practical platform for optimizing stem regeneration‐based genetic modification systems.

title:
Single‐cell transcriptome atlas reveals a

authors:
Lingli Li, 
Ye Xu, 
Wei Liu, 
Zhitao Niu, 
Qingyun Xue, 
Xiaoyu Ding
abstract:
SUMMARY 
                   
                    Plants employ cell‐type‐specific transcriptional programs to defend against pathogens, yet the cellular heterogeneity of immune responses in the medicinal orchid
                     Dendrobium officinale 
                    Kimura et Migo remains largely unexplored. A single‐cell transcriptomic atlas of the
                     D. officinale 
                    stem base upon
                     Sclerotium rolfsii 
                    infection was constructed, profiling over 20 000 cells across 12 and 24 h post‐infection. A total of 21 cell clusters were resolved into 6 major cell types—epidermal, ground tissue parenchyma, proliferating, xylem, phloem, and vascular bundle parenchyma cells—with identities validated by fluorescence
                     in situ 
                    hybridization. Cell‐type‐specific analyses revealed that epidermal and phloem cells mounted early defense responses, while xylem cells exhibited the most extensive transcriptional reprogramming at 24 hpi, coinciding with the activation of lignin biosynthesis pathways.
                     WRKY33 
                    was identified as a central transcriptional activator that directly binds W‐box motifs in the promoters of lignin biosynthetic genes
                     C4H 
                    and
                     HCT 
                    , promoting lignin deposition and enhancing disease resistance. Conversely, the nuclear‐localized chaperone
                     HSP81 
                    physically interacts with
                     WRKY33 
                    and functions as a broad regulator of multiple transcription factors via co‐factor sequestration, thereby compromising defense when overexpressed. These findings uncover a
                     WRKY33 
                    ‐
                     HSP81 
                    regulatory module that orchestrates phenylpropanoid‐mediated defense in
                     D. officinale 
                    , providing a high‐resolution cellular framework for understanding plant immunity and offering potential targets for improving disease resistance in this economically valuable species.

title:
Nuclear importin α1
                     AtIMPA1 
                    regulates stomatal reopening to defend against
                     Pst 
                     DC3000

authors:
Ting Zhang, 
Kang Wang, 
Yi Guan, 
Jingao Zhang, 
Charles Tetteh, 
Chenxi Liu, 
Cheng Zhang, 
Pinyuan Jin, 
Sheng Luo, 
Yiling Wang, 
Huajian Zhang
abstract:
SUMMARY 
                   
                    Importin α family proteins serve as essential carriers for transporting specific disease‐resistant proteins into the nucleus, enabling these proteins to function properly. However, whether importin α proteins are involved in plant immunity remains unclear. Here, we characterized a guard cell‐expressed protein importin α1 AtIMPA1, which contributed to resistance against
                     Pseudomonas syringae 
                    pv.
                     tomato 
                    DC3000 (
                     Pst 
                    DC3000). When dip‐inoculated with
                     Pst 
                    DC3000, the
                     impa1 
                    mutants exhibited increased susceptibility, along with significant stomatal reopening induced by the phytotoxin coronatine (COR) secreted by
                     Pst 
                    DC3000; while overexpression of
                     AtIMPA1 
                    enhanced resistance to
                     Pst 
                    DC3000 with compromised stomatal reopening induced by COR. Notably, following syringe‐infiltration of
                     Pst 
                    DC3000, the
                     impa1 
                    mutants showed increased resistance, whereas overexpression lines were more susceptible to
                     Pst 
                    DC3000, indicating that COR‐triggered stomatal reopening is a primary determinant in AtIMPA1‐mediated disease resistance. Further investigations revealed that AtIMPA1 regulated COR‐triggered stomatal reopening is linked to abscisic acid (ABA) signaling. Mutation of
                     AtIMPA1 
                    attenuated the ABA‐mediated inhibition of root length and seed germination, and disrupted the ABA‐induced protein abundance and localization of the ABA‐responsive protein, supporting its role in regulating the ABA response. These findings shed light on the functional significance of AtIMPA1 in COR‐triggered stomatal reopening and provided new insights into how importin α proteins orchestrate ABA signaling to regulate plant immunity.

title: Sorghum Metabolic Atlas: A fluorescent protein‐based subcellular localization resource for sorghum enzymes
authors:
Purva Karia, 
William P. Dwyer, 
Ava Kloss‐Schmidt, 
Charles Hawkins, 
Bo Xue, 
Daniel Ginzburg, 
Maxine L. Gutierrez, 
Ritesh Mewalal, 
Ian Blaby, 
David W. Ehrhardt, 
Seung Y. Rhee
abstract:
SUMMARY 
                   
                    Plant metabolism drives traits essential for productivity and resilience, yet understanding metabolic networks requires subcellular, cellular, and tissue‐level spatial context that remains limited, particularly in crop species. Experimentally derived subcellular localization data for enzymes are sparse, constraining analyses of metabolic organization in the cell. We developed a high‐throughput protoplast transformation and fluorescent protein (FP) tagging system optimized for
                     Sorghum bicolor 
                    , a climate‐resilient C
                     4 
                    crop. Using this platform, we experimentally determined the subcellular localization of 234 metabolic enzymes spanning 184 pathways. The sorghum enzymes we characterized localize to 12 subcellular compartments. Comparison with computational predictions highlights variable accuracy across compartments, and cross‐species comparison with
                     Arabidopsis thaliana 
                    shows partial agreement with available experimental data. All data are accessible through the Sorghum Metabolic Atlas (
                     www.sorghummetabolicatlas.org 
                    ) web platform, enabling search, visualization, and download. This study presents a large‐scale experimental dataset of enzyme localization in sorghum, providing a resource for studies of plant metabolic organization and comparative analyses.
